However, these methods often place greater focus on more effectively modelling the historical series, largely neglecting the forecasting phase, which generates long-term forecasts by separately predicting multiple time points. Given that real-world time series typically consist of various long short-term dynamics, independent predictions over individual time points may fail to express complex underlying patterns and can lead to a lack of global views. To address these issues, this work explores new perspectives from the forecasting phase and proposes a novel Implicit Forecaster (IF) as an additional decoding module. Inspired by decomposition forecasting, IF adopts a more nuanced approach by implicitly predicting constituent waves represented by their frequency, amplitude, and phase, thereby accurately forming the time series. Extensive experimental results from multiple real-world datasets show that IF can consistently boost mainstream time series models, achieving state-of-the-art forecasting performance. And based on this idea, we propose a powerful decomposition-based enhancement framework, namely DecompNet. Our method converts the time series decomposition into an implicit process, where it can give a time series model the decomposition-related knowledge during inference, even though this model does not actually decompose the input time series. Thus, our DecompNet can enable a model to inherit the performance promotion brought by time series decomposition but will not introduce any additional inference costs, successfully enhancing the model performance while enjoying better efficiency. Experimentally, our DecompNet exhibits promising enhancement capability and compelling framework generality. Especially, it can also enhance the performance of the latest and state-of-the-art models, greatly pushing the performance limit of time series forecasting. Through comprehensive comparisons, DecompNet also shows excellent performance and efficiency superiority, making the decomposition-based enhancement framework surpass the well-recognized normalization-based frameworks for the first time.       "text": "NeurIPS Poster Selective Learning for Deep Time Series Forecasting NeurIPS 2025\n\nPoster Thu, Dec 4, 2025 • 11:00 AM – 2:00 PM PST\n\n# Selective Learning for Deep Time Series Forecasting\n\nYisong Fu ⋅ Zezhi Shao ⋅ Chengqing Yu ⋅ Yujie Li ⋅ Zhulin An ⋅ Qi Wang ⋅ Yongjun Xu ⋅ Fei Wang\n\n### Abstract\n\nBenefiting from high capacity for capturing complex temporal patterns, deep learning (DL) has significantly advanced time series forecasting (TSF). However, deep models tend to suffer from severe overfitting due to the inherent vulnerability of time series to noise and anomalies. The prevailing DL paradigm uniformly optimizes all timesteps through the MSE loss and learns those uncertain and anomalous timesteps without difference, ultimately resulting in overfitting. To address this, we propose a novel selective learning strategy for deep TSF. Specifically, selective learning screens a subset of the whole timesteps to calculate the MSE loss in optimization, guiding the model to focus on generalizable timesteps while disregarding non-generalizable ones. Our framework introduces a dual-mask mechanism to target timesteps: (1) an uncertainty mask leveraging residual entropy to filter uncertain timesteps, and (2) an anomaly mask employing residual lower bound estimation to exclude anomalous timesteps. Extensive experiments across eight real-world datasets demonstrate that selective learning can significantly improve the predictive performance for typical state-of-the-art deep models, including 37.4% MSE reduction for Informer, 8.4% for TimesNet, and 6.5% for iTransformer.\n\nShow more\n\n### Video\n\nChat is not available.\n\nSuccessful Page Load",

```
      "text": "NeurIPS Towards Efficient Foundation Model: A Novel Time Series Embedding NeurIPS 2025\n\nPoster in Workshop: ML x OR: Mathematical Foundations and Operational Integration of Machine Learning for Uncertainty-Aware Decision-Making\n\n# Towards Efficient Foundation Model: A Novel Time Series Embedding\n\nJessy Xinyi Han ⋅ Arth Dharaskar ⋅ Nathaniel Lanier ⋅ Abdullah Alomar ⋅ Aditya Agrawal ⋅ Angela Yuan ⋅ Jocelyn Hsieh ⋅ Ishan Shah ⋅ Muhammad Amjad ⋅ Devavrat Shah\n\nProject Page [OpenReview]\n\n### Abstract\n\nTime Series Foundation Model (TSFM) learns appropriate embeddings from pre-training data and uses them to embed the input time series for in-context learning to produce forecast. TSFM requires rich pre-training dataset and large computational resources to learn effective embeddings. In contrast, traditional time series modeling paradigm generates forecast for a given time series by fitting one of many pre-determined models and using the best of them to produce a forecast. Though resource efficient, it suffers from inability to utilize the pre-training data along with the challenges involved in the best model selection. In this work, we are motivated to bring the best of both worlds together to enable resource efficient TSFM approach. Towards that, we introduce a novel embedding of time series of any length and scale by mapping them to unit square (i.e $[0, 1]^2$) or equivalently a 2D image. To evaluate its efficacy compared to embedding from a TSFM, we consider the task of model identification or classification for dataset where each time series is generated from one of many pre-determined model class. We find that the performance of the proposed embeddings is comparable to that of embeddings from a pre-trained TSFM, but at a fraction of resource requirement. This suggests an alternative architectural possibility for a compute efficient TSFM.\n\nShow more\n\nChat is not available.\n\nSuccessful Page Load",

      "text": "NeurIPS Poster MIRA: Medical Time Series Foundation Model for Real-World Health Data NeurIPS 2025\n\nPoster Wed, Dec 3, 2025 • 4:30 PM – 7:30 PM PST\n\n# MIRA: Medical Time Series Foundation Model for Real-World Health Data\n\nHao Li ⋅ Bowen Deng ⋅ Chang Xu ⋅ ZhiYuan Feng ⋅ Viktor Schlegel ⋅ Yu-Hao Huang ⋅ Yizheng Sun ⋅ Jingyuan Sun ⋅ Kailai Yang ⋅ Yiyao Yu ⋅ Jiang Bian\n\n[Poster] [OpenReview]\n\n### Abstract\n\nA unified foundation model for medical time series—pretrained on open access and ethically reviewed medical corpora—offers the potential to reduce annotation burdens, minimize model customization, and enable robust transfer across clinical institutions, modalities, and tasks, particularly in data-scarce or privacy-constrained environments. However, existing time series foundation models struggle to handle medical time series data due to its inherent challenges, including irregular intervals, heterogeneous sampling rates, and frequent missingness. To address these challenges, we introduce MIRA, a unified foundation model specifically designed for medical time series forecasting. MIRA incorporates a Continuous-Time Rotary Positional Encoding that enables fine-grained modeling of variable time intervals, a frequency-specific mixture-of-experts layer that routes computation across latent frequency regimes to further promote temporal specialization, and a Continuous Dynamics Extrapolation Block based on Neural ODE that models the continuous trajectory of latent states, enabling accurate forecasting at arbitrary target timestamps. Pretrained on a large-scale and diverse medical corpus comprising over 454 billion time points collect from publicly available datasets, MIRA achieving reductions in forecasting errors by an average of 8% and 6% in out-of-distribution and in-distribution scenarios, respectively. We also introduce a comprehensive benchmark spanning multiple downstream clinical tasks, establishing a foundation for future research in medical time series modeling.\n\nShow more\n\n### Video\n\nChat is not available.\n\nSuccessful Page Load",

      "text": "Recent Advances in Time Series Foundation Models: Have We Reached the ‘BERT Moment’? NeurIPS 2025 \n\n \n\n \n\n- San Diego\n- Sydney\n- Atlanta\n- Mexico City\n\n \n\n \n\n \n\nWorkshop Sun, Dec 7, 2025 • 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM PST\n\n \n\n \n\n# Recent Advances in Time Series Foundation Models: Have We Reached the ‘BERT Moment’?\n\n \n\nThomas Moreau · Romain Tavenard · Valentina Zantedeschi · Vasilii Feofanov · Ievgen Redko · Ambroise Odonnat\n\n \n\nProject Page [OpenReview]\n\n \n\n### Abstract\n\nFoundation models (FMs) have achieved great success in NLP and vision, inspiring over 20 new time series FMs (TSFMs) in the past year. Despite promising results, studies show that carefully designed lightweight supervised baselines often match TSFM performance. Unlike NLP’s “BERT Moment,” TSFMs still require full fine-tuning to be competitive in real-world scenarios. Additionally, some tabular FMs rival TSFMs without being time series-specific. Recent benchmarks also provide mixed evidence: GIFT-Eval favors TSFMs, OpenTS shows statistical models outperforming deep learning on univariate data, and FoundTS finds supervised baselines on par with TSFMs. This workshop aims to bring together researchers to examine the gap between TSFM potential and real-world utility, and to identify benchmarks and applications where TSFMs can truly excel. The key topics of this workshop include, but are not limited to: - Benchmarking Foundation Models in Time Series, - Scaling Laws and Efficiency in Time Series Models, - Evaluating Transferability and Adaptability of Foundation Models, - Leveraging Foundation Models of Other Modalities for Time Series, - Unsupervised performance estimation of TSFMs, - Industrial Benchmarking of Time Series Foundation Models More details are provided in our Call for Papers.\n\nShow more\n\n \n\n### Video\n\n \n\nChat is not available.\n\n \n\n### Schedule\n\nTimezone: America/Los_Angeles\n\n8:30 AM\n\nWelcome and introduction\n\nThomas Moreau · Ievgen Redko · Romain Tavenard · Ambroise Odonnat · Vasilii Feofanov · Valentina Zantedeschi\n\nVideo\n\n8:45 AM\n\nVertical AI Meets Observability\n\nAmeet Talwalkar\n\nVideo\n\nLink\n\n9:20 AM\n\nFrom Time Series Foundation Model to Reasoning and Agentic Systems: A Roadmap for Emergent Anomaly Detection Intelligence\n\nChenghao Liu\n\nVideo\n\nLink\n\n9:50 AM\n\nCoffe break\n\n10:10 AM\n\nEfficiently Generating Correlated Sample Paths from Multi-step Time Series Foundation Models\n\nEthan Baron · Boris Oreshkin · Ruijun Ma · Hanyu Zhang · Kari Torkkola · Michael Mahoney · Andrew Wilson · Tatiana Konstantinova\n\nVideo\n\nLink\n\n10:25 AM\n\nPre-trained Forecasting Models: Strong Zero-Shot Feature Extractors for Time Series Classification\n\nAndreas Auer · Daniel Klotz · Sebastian Böck · Sepp Hochreiter\n\nVideo\n\nLink\n\n10:40 AM\n\nPoster Session 1\n\n→ LLM-Integrated Bayesian State Space Models for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting\n\nSungjun Cho · Changho Shin · Suenggwan Jo · Xinya Yan · Shourjo Chaudhuri · Frederic Sala\n\nLink\n\n→ TimeSeriesExamAgent: Creating TimeSeries Reasoning Benchmarks at Scale\n\nMalg",

      "text": "FlowState: Sampling-Rate Invariant Time Series Foundation Model with Dynamic Forecasting Horizons for NeurIPS 2025 - IBM Research\n\n## Abstract\n\nFoundation models (FMs) have transformed natural language processing (NLP), but their successes have not yet translated to the time series domain. Existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) struggle with generalization across varying context and target lengths, lack adaptability to different sampling rates, and are computationally inefficient. We introduce FlowState, a novel TSFM architecture that addresses these challenges through two key innovations: a state space model (SSM) based encoder and a functional basis decoder. This design enables continuous-time modeling, adjustment to various sampling rates, and flexible forecasting horizons without retraining. We further propose a parallel training strategy that enhances robustness and accelerates training. Despite being the smallest model, FlowState achieves state-of-the-art results on the GIFT-ZS and the Chronos-ZS benchmarks, while demonstrating superior adaptability to unseen sampling rates.\n\n## Related\n\nWorkshop paper\n\n### End-to-End Learning for Information Gathering\n\nRares Christian, Pavithra Harsha, et al.\n\nNeurIPS 2025\n\nConference paper\n\n### Keeping an Eye on LLM Unlearning: The Hidden Risk and Remedy\n\nJie Ren, Zhenwei Dai, et al.\n\nNeurIPS 2025\n\nWorkshop paper\n\n### Representation Similarity Reveals Implicit Layer Grouping in Neural Networks\n\nTian Gao, Amit Dhurandhar, et al.\n\nNeurIPS 2025\n\nConference paper\n\n### Cross-Domain Telemetry Architecture: Real-Time Metrics in the Computing Continuum\n\nJose Manuel Bernabe' Murcia, Eduardo Canovas Martinez, et al.\n\nMobiSec 2024\n\nView all publications",

      "url": "https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/130462",
      "text": "NeurIPS How Foundational are Foundation Models for Time Series Forecasting? NeurIPS 2025 \n\n \n\n \n\n- San Diego\n- Mexico City\n\n \n\n \n\n \n\nPoster in Workshop: Recent Advances in Time Series Foundation Models: Have We Reached the ‘BERT Moment’? Sun, Dec 7, 2025 • 10:40 AM – 11:40 AM PST\n\n \n\n \n\n# How Foundational are Foundation Models for Time Series Forecasting?\n\n \n\nNouha KARAOULI · Denis Coquenet · Elisa Fromont · Martial Mermillod · REYBOZ\n\n \n\nProject Page [OpenReview] \n\n \n\n### Abstract\n\nFoundation Models are designed to serve as versatile embedding machines, with strong zero shot capabilities and superior generalization performance when fine-tuned on diverse downstream tasks. While this is largely true for language and vision foundation models, we argue that the inherent diversity of time series data makes them less suited for building effective foundation models. We demonstrate this using forecasting as our downstream task. We show that the zero-shot capabilities of a time series foundation model are significantly influenced and tied to the specific domains it has been pretrained on. Furthermore, when applied to unseen real-world time series data, fine-tuned foundation models do not consistently yield substantially better results, relative to their increased parameter count and memory footprint, than smaller, dedicated models tailored to the specific forecasting task at hand.\n\nShow more\n\n \n\n \n\nChat is not available.\n\n \n\n \n\n",

    {
      "id": "https://openreview.net/forum?id=YngHXbJM8g",
      "title": "SEMPO: Lightweight Foundation Models for Time Series Forecasting | OpenReview",
      "url": "https://openreview.net/forum?id=YngHXbJM8g",
      "text": "SEMPO: Lightweight Foundation Models for Time Series Forecasting | OpenReview\n\n## SEMPO: Lightweight Foundation Models for Time Series Forecasting\n\n### Hui He, Kun Yi, Yuanchi Ma, Qi Zhang, Zhendong Niu, Guansong Pang \n\nNeurIPS 2025 posterEveryone Revisions BibTeX CC BY 4.0\n\nKeywords: time series, foundation model, forecasting, lightweight\n\nTL;DR: SEMPO is a lightweight time series foundation model with energy-aware spectral decomposition and mixture-of-prompts enabled Transformer for effective and efficient zero-shot and few-shot forecasting.\n\nAbstract: The recent boom of large pre-trained models witnesses remarkable success in developing foundation models (FMs) for time series forecasting. Despite impressive performance across diverse downstream forecasting tasks, existing time series FMs possess massive network architectures and require substantial pre-training on large-scale datasets, which significantly hinders their deployment in resource-constrained environments. In response to this growing tension between versatility and affordability, we propose **SEMPO**, a novel lightweight foundation model that requires pretraining on relatively small-scale data, yet exhibits strong general time series forecasting. Concretely, SEMPO comprises two key modules: 1) _energy-aware **S**p**E**ctral decomposition module_, that substantially improves the utilization of pre-training data by modeling not only the high-energy frequency signals but also the low-energy yet informative frequency signals that are ignored in current methods; and 2) _**M**ixture-of-**P**r**O**mpts enabled Transformer_, that learns heterogeneous temporal patterns through small dataset-specific prompts and adaptively routes time series tokens to prompt-based experts for parameter-efficient model adaptation across different datasets and domains. Equipped with these modules, SEMPO significantly reduces both pre-training data scale and model size, while achieving strong generalization. Extensive experiments on two large-scale benchmarks covering 16 datasets demonstrate the superior performance of SEMPO in both zero-shot and few-shot forecasting scenarios compared with state-of-the-art methods. Code and data are available at https://github.com/mala-lab/SEMPO.\n\nPrimary Area: Deep learning (e.g., architectures, generative models, optimization for deep networks, foundation models, LLMs)\n\nSubmission Number: 15850\n\nLoading",
```

```
      "text": "Toto: Time Series Optimized Transformer for Observability Technical Report\n\n# Toto: Time Series Optimized Transformer for Observability Technical Report\n\nBen Cohen Emaad Khwaja Kan Wang Charles Masson \\ANDElise Ramé Youssef Doubli Othmane Abou-Amal \\ANDme {ben.cohen, emaad, kan.wang, charles.masson, elise.rame, youssef.doubli, othmane}@ datadoghq.com\n\n###### Abstract\n\nThis technical report describes the Time Series Optimized Transformer for Observability (Toto), a new state-of-the-art foundation model for time series forecasting developed by Datadog. In addition to advancing the state of the art on generalized time series benchmarks in domains such as electricity and weather, this model is the first general-purpose time series forecasting foundation model to be specifically tuned for observability metrics.\n\nToto was trained on a dataset of one trillion time series data points – the largest among all currently published time series foundation models. Alongside publicly available time series datasets, 75% of the data used to train Toto consists of fully anonymous numerical metric data points from the Datadog platform.\n\nIn our experiments, Toto outperforms existing time series foundation models on observability data. It does this while also excelling at general-purpose forecasting tasks, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on multiple open benchmark datasets.\n\nIn this report, we detail the following key contributions:\n\n•\n\nProportional factorized space-time attention: We introduce an advanced attention mechanism that allows for efficient grouping of multivariate time series features, reducing computational overhead while maintaining high accuracy.\n\n•\n\nStudent-T mixture model head: This novel use of a probabilistic model that robustly generalizes Gaussian mixture models enables Toto to more accurately capture the complex dynamics of time series data and provides superior performance over traditional approaches.\n\n•\n\nDomain-specific training data: In addition to general multi-domain time series data, Toto is specifically pre-trained on a large-scale dataset of Datadog observability metrics, encompassing unique characteristics not present in open-source datasets. This targeted training ensures enhanced performance in observability metric forecasting.\n\nFigure 1: Toto architecture diagram. Input time series of $T$ steps (univariate example used for simplicity here) are first embedded using the patch embedding layer. They then pass through the transformer stack, which contains $L$ identical segments. Each segment of the transformer consists of one space-wise transformer block followed by $N$ time-wise blocks. The flattened transformer outputs are projected to form the parameters of the Student-T mixture model (SMM) head. The final outputs are the forecasts for the input series, shifted $P$ steps (the patch width) into the future.\n\n## 1 Background\n\nFigure 2: Example of Toto's 96-step zero-shot forecasts on the ETTh1 dataset, showing multivariate",
```

```
34	\title{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters: Bypassing Routing Collapse in Normalized Time Series Foundation Models}
35

51	
52	\maketitle
53	
54	\begin{abstract}
55	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT and Moirai provide powerful pretrained representations, but adapting them to a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions. Standard TSFM benchmarks use a single static head---one adapter topology for every input window. A natural improvement is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter, where a router selects the best expert head for each window. However, on TSFMs with instance normalization, this \textbf{catastrophically fails}: the router learns to send \emph{every} window to the \emph{same} expert---routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$, and the remaining experts are never used. We identify \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse}: instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states that all look alike. Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---and all five standard MoE-rescue families (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) across eleven configurations fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism and yields a signal-ratio predictor ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) that identifies where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does \emph{not} (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$) on the primary backbone and generalizing across four additional backbones (two negative controls without instance normalization confirm specificity). A predicted consequence---the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}---is confirmed: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$, because unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse. A third architecture (\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}}) restoring raw-signal access at the expert level matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets (Appendix).
56	\end{abstract}
57	
58	\section{Introduction}
59	\label{sec:intro}
60	
61	{\looseness=-1 Time series foundation models (TSFMs)---MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, and others~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}---provide powerful pretrained representations, now scaling to billions of parameters with internal MoE routing. A practical question determines deployment utility: \textit{how should the adapter that connects the backbone to a downstream task be designed?}}
62	
63	\textbf{The problem with one-size-fits-all adapters.} Today, every public TSFM benchmark adapts the backbone with a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. But real time series are non-stationary---ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions---and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable expert.
64	
65	\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?} Frozen-backbone adaptation is compatible with established multi-tenant adapter deployment regimes~\citep{houlsby2019adapters,hu2022lora}---regimes that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot serve. A single TSFM in GPU VRAM can serve thousands of tenants via 426K-parameter adapters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB each) swapped in microseconds---eliminating $O(N)$ independent training pipelines. On-device deployment and cross-task reuse impose similar constraints (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes an increasingly important per-dataset adaptation path.
66	
67	\textbf{The collapse problem.} This natural mixture-of-experts approach \emph{catastrophically fails} on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The root cause is \textbf{normalization-induced co-adaptation}: the dominant expert receives larger gradients, which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, creating a feedback loop that collapses within ${\sim}50$ training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). Even with a frozen backbone, hidden-state routing still underperforms because RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish different input regimes. This is instance-normalization-specific: Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does \emph{not} collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}).
68	
69	\textbf{Our fix.} Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen. Only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. Eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) all fail to recover performance ($2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA across 720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), confirming that the problem is in the router's \emph{input}, not its \emph{optimization}.
70	
71	Our contributions are threefold:
72	
73	\textbf{(1)~A principle validated across three normalization families and two modalities: instance normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.} A mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) shows that instance normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics. The principle makes four \textbf{testable predictions}, all confirmed: (a)~$R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); (b)~backbones without instance normalization should not collapse (Timer-XL, Chronos; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}); (c)~cross-modality transfer (ViT$+$InstanceNorm1d collapses; ResNet does not; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); (d)~a phase-transition threshold $\alpha^* {=} R/(R{+}1) {\approx} 0.40$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition}, Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}). Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories: MOMENT collapses ($0.60{\to}0.00$) while Timer-XL \emph{rises} ($1.49{\to}1.60$)---same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
74	
75	\textbf{(2)~Fix and a predicted consequence.} Because the principle pinpoints the cause, the fix follows directly: RR-MoA routes on raw pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The principle also predicts a \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning---confirmed at $12$--$79\%$ across all six datasets. RR-MoA generalizes across four RevIN/LayerNorm backbones; two negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) confirm instance-normalization-specificity.
76	
77	\textbf{(3)~Actionable diagnosis.} The diagnosis is further validated by its predictive power: a third architecture, \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}), restores raw-signal access at the \emph{expert} level via a shared NLinear branch added to each expert's output. This closes the gap to supervised baselines, matching or beating DLinear on 6/6 datasets at $H{=}96$ ($107/123$ cells across six backbones; \S\ref{sec:main_results}).
78	
79	\section{Related Work}
80	
81	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
82	
83	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
84	
85	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.
86	
87	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental, and \citet{zou2025ibnorm} argue that variance-centric normalization (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) is suboptimal for representation learning because two representations with identical mean and variance can encode different amounts of task-relevant information. We identify a specific, mechanistic consequence of this principle that has not been characterized in the MoE literature: when the stripped statistics carry the \emph{routing} signal in a downstream MoE adapter, instance normalization causes catastrophic routing collapse---a failure mode distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE rescue literature.}
88	
89	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
90	
91	\section{Method}
92	\label{sec:method}
```

```
# Concrete Writing Critique: NeurIPS Style vs Your Manuscript

The supervisor is **substantially right**. The paper has the technical substance of a NeurIPS submission, but the prose is structurally closer to a lab tech-report than to the two NeurIPS 2025 TS papers I read end-to-end (SRSNet, SEMPO). Below: 6 specific style differences with verbatim quotes, then 7 surgical rewrites.

---

## 1) Bold-paragraph-headings vs. flowing prose

**SRSNet's intro (no bold-headings at all):**

> "However, the commonly-used adjacent patching technique, i.e., with fixed stride, divides patches on different contextual time series with the same positions, which results in a fixed representation space. Though multi-scale modeling [...] may create several representation spaces with different patch sizes, the fixed strides also limit the potential. Because fixed representation spaces assume that all information useful for forecasting is evenly distributed in the contextual time series. As shown in the upper part of Figure 1, the assumption is broken due to the phenomenons of changeable periods, shifting, and anomalies."

**SEMPO's intro (no bold-headings either):**

> "However, excessively large pre-trained models often impose substantial computational burdens during both training and inference, hindering its application to computational resource-constrained environments [23, 24]. This motivates the question: Can we instead devise 'small' FMs to serve as an alternative to these 'large' FMs..."

**Your intro (lines 63-69)** uses five bold-paragraph-headings in five paragraphs:

> `\textbf{The problem with one-size-fits-all adapters.}` ... `\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?}` ... `\textbf{The collapse problem.}` ... `\textbf{Our fix.}`

**What's different.** Neither NeurIPS paper uses bold-paragraph-headings in the intro. They flow paragraph-to-paragraph through transitions ("However...", "To answer this question...", "In line with this trend..."). Your bold headings act as bullet-list bullets in disguise, which is exactly what makes the paper read like a tech report. Bold-paragraph-headings are common in *method* sections (SEMPO uses them in §3.3 "Energy-wise Spectral Partitioning", "Frequency-wise Spectral Masking") but **not in the introduction**. NeurIPS reviewers read intros as narrative; yours reads as a press release.

---

## 2) Numerical density per sentence

**SEMPO's headline-claim sentence (in conclusion):**

> "...with only 6.5M parameters pre-trained on 83M time points, surpasses SOTA time series FMs with hundreds of millions of parameters pre-trained on billions of time points, demonstrating an average reduction of 12% and 22% in forecasting errors under zero- and few-shot scenarios, respectively."

That is **two** numbers per sentence, each load-bearing.

**Your abstract (line 55), one sentence:**

> "Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---and all five standard MoE-rescue families (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) across eleven configurations fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs)."

That's **eight** numbers in one sentence: 8, 1.49, 1.60, 0.60, 0.00, 5, 11, 2.7, 720. The reader cannot retain them. NeurIPS abstracts *summarise* the headline; tech reports *log* the evidence.

**Same problem in your contribution-1 (line 73):** $\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$, $\alpha^*{=}R/(R{+}1){\approx}0.40$, $0.60{\to}0.00$, $1.49{\to}1.60$ — all in a single contribution bullet. SRSNet's contributions (last paragraph of §1) contain **zero numbers**.

---

## 3) Contribution lists: "(1)(2)(3)" vs. interpretive bullets

**SRSNet's contributions:**

> "• We propose a modular SRS, which efficiently and adaptively constructs the selective representation space to fully exploit the information in the contextual time series, and is able to improve the performance of patch-based models in a simple plug-and-play paradigm.
> • Technically, we devise the Selective Patching and Dynamic Reassembly techniques, which are able to constitute a selective representation space at the patch perspective. And they are easily to be optimized through gradient-based strategies.
> • Applying SRS with an MLP forms a simple-yet-effective method, called SRSNet."

**SEMPO's contributions:**

> "• We propose SEMPO, a novel time series FM with significantly reduced model size and pre-training scale, yet demonstrating superior generalization ability...
> • We reveal the bias towards high-energy frequency signals in the pre-training of current solutions and introduce the EASD module to mitigate this bias..."

**Your contributions (lines 73-77):**

> `\textbf{(1)~A principle validated across three normalization families and two modalities: instance normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.}` A mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) shows...

**What's different.** Both NeurIPS papers' contribution bullets are 1-2 sentences, **conceptual**, and contain no numbers. Yours has **bold headlines containing the entire contribution sentence** followed by a paragraph of nested numbered sub-claims `(a)(b)(c)(d)`, each with statistics. Your contribution-1 contains 4 sub-bullets and 5 numerical claims; SRSNet's longest contribution has 0. This is the single biggest "tech report" tell.

---

## 4) Theory presentation: hedged-narrative vs. theorem-environment block

**SEMPO does not present a theorem at all** in §3.3 — the energy-bias claim is justified citationally ("the Transformer backbones widely used in time series FMs [...] often exhibit an energy bias [41]") and then operationalised. **SRSNet** doesn't state a theorem either; the universal-approximation appeal is one inline sentence.

**Your theory presentation (lines 481-494):**

> `\begin{observation}[Routing Information Loss Under Instance Normalization]`
> ...four nested sub-claims (i)(ii)(iii)(iv) with footnote at end.

The Observation environment with 4 sub-claims and inline ${\pm}0.26$ nats KSG cross-checks reads like a lemma in an information-theory paper. Neither NeurIPS TS paper uses a theorem environment. **This is not automatically wrong**, but the surrounding prose needs to *earn* the theorem with intuition first — yours jumps directly into the formal statement without a soft motivating paragraph. SEMPO motivates EASD with a 2-paragraph narrative on energy bias before any equation. You motivate Observation 1 with one transitional sentence (line 479: "We now formalize it through an information-theoretic lens"), then drop a 4-part formal statement.

---

## 5) "We do X. We do Y. We do Z." cadence

**SEMPO (paragraph from §3.3):**

> "We then perform spectral partitioning in the energy axis by adjusting a learnable energy threshold τ according to the input's spectral characteristics to delineate high- and low-energy components. This separation ensures low-energy components are not overwhelmed by high-energy components, thus enabling the extraction of frequency-localized patterns for modeling complex temporal dynamics."

Two sentences: one declarative *what we do*, one explaining *why it works*. The paragraph **argues**.

**Your §4.1 (line 267):**

> "This section proceeds in four steps: we first show that RR-MoA consistently outperforms fixed adapters (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}), then diagnose why standard MoE routing fails (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}), demonstrate that no standard rescue mechanism recovers performance (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), and finally compare against a comprehensive baseline suite (Table~\ref{tab:baselines})."

This is a pure roadmap sentence with four parallel clauses, each pointing to a table. NeurIPS papers prefer a single thesis sentence ("This section establishes that...") followed by paragraphs that *argue* for that thesis, with tables introduced in passing. The roadmap-to-tables structure is characteristic of an **internal report**, not a publishable manuscript.

---

## 6) Parenthetical and citation density

**SRSNet method (random sample):**

> "Inspired by the aboved motivations, we propose SRS, a plug-and-play module to efficiently construct the Selective Representation Space for contextual time series. Technically, we propose the Selective Patching to select the patches from the contextual time series, and utilize the Dynamic Reassembly to determine the sequence of patches."

**Your line 61 (one sentence, opening of the intro):**

> "Time series foundation models (TSFMs)---MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, and others~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}---provide powerful pretrained representations..."

Eleven citations interrupt a single sentence. SRSNet's first sentence has **zero** citations. SEMPO's opening has **one citation cluster** on the second sentence ([1]–[4]). Your opener tries to do 5+ jobs at once: introduce TSFMs, list six families, signal MoE awareness, and frame deployment scope. NeurIPS papers slow down — first sentence is a thesis, citations come later.

---

## What the NeurIPS papers do that yours doesn't

1. **Single motivating example before formalism.** SRSNet's Figure 1 shows "Adjacent vs Selective Patching" with a stylized example *before* any equation. SEMPO's Figure 1 shows ChronosS missing low-energy components *before* defining EASD. Your Figure 1 (`fig:framework`, line 94) shows the **architecture** of the proposed method, not the **phenomenon** it diagnoses. A NeurIPS-style move would be: lead with a 2-panel cartoon of the routing-collapse phenomenon (entropy time-series + expert-assignment scatter) *before* introducing RR-MoA.

2. **Hedging in theory.** SEMPO writes "often exhibit an energy bias [41]" — the *often* + citation pattern. Your Observation 1 sub-claim (iv) contains 9 absolute statements in a row with no hedging.

3. **Soft transitions.** SEMPO transitions paragraphs with "To accommodate a wide range of...", "To address this issue...", "Despite simultaneously alleviating...". Your transitions are bold paragraph-headings — a hard cut, not a flowing connector.

4. **Conclusion that synthesizes.** SRSNet's conclusion (one paragraph, ~120 words) is purely interpretive. Your conclusion (haven't read it explicitly but the abstract foreshadows it) appears to recap numerical results — verify this and rewrite if so.

5. **Limitations as essay paragraphs, not bullets.** SRSNet's "Potential limitations" has 4 bullets each of which is **3-5 full sentences with reasoning**. The bullets are essay-paragraphs in disguise. NeurIPS reviewers reward this.

---

## Seven surgical rewrites

**(R1) Line 55, abstract sentence "Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly...".** Cut the parenthetical "(Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)" from the abstract and the abstract's "$2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs". Move all of these to §4. Rewrite as: *"Eight causal controls converge on the same mechanism, and five standard MoE-rescue families fail to recover performance."* SRSNet's abstract has zero numbers in its problem-statement sentences and only `≤2 layers` in the method sentence.

**(R2) Lines 63-69, replace the four bold-paragraph-headings with flowing transitions.** Specifically: delete `\textbf{The problem with one-size-fits-all adapters.}`, `\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?}`, `\textbf{The collapse problem.}`, `\textbf{Our fix.}`. Reconnect with: "Today's TSFM benchmarks adapt the backbone with a single static head [...]. **However**, real time series are non-stationary [...]. A natural remedy is a mixture of expert adapters. **This natural approach catastrophically fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization** [...]. **Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix follows directly:** RR-MoA routes on raw input." Pattern: SEMPO's "However... To answer this question... In line with this trend..." cadence.

**(R3) Lines 73-77 contributions block.** Replace numbered `(1)(2)(3)` with three bullet-points each ≤ 2 sentences and **zero embedded numbers**. SRSNet model:
- "We identify *normalization-induced routing collapse*: a failure mode of MoE adapters on TSFMs that use instance normalization, distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE rescue literature."
- "We formalize the mechanism via a mutual-information decomposition that yields a signal-ratio predictor identifying which datasets benefit from raw routing — including boundary cases where it does not."
- "We propose RR-MoA, a minimal architectural fix that routes on raw pre-normalization input, and validate the underlying principle across three architectures, five backbones, and two modalities."

Move the $54/54$, $\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $12{-}79\%$, etc. *out of contributions* and into §4.

**(R4) Line 61 opening sentence.** Cut the 11-citation cluster from sentence 1. Move citations to a "TSFMs include MOMENT [...], Chronos [...], Moirai [...], Timer-XL [...], and others." structured second sentence. SRSNet's opener has zero citations: *"Time series organize data points chronologically and are either univariate or multivariate."*

**(R5) Line 267 roadmap sentence.** Delete it. NeurIPS sections do not announce their structure with "This section proceeds in four steps". Replace with a thesis sentence: *"RR-MoA's advantage rests on three claims: that fixed adapters are suboptimal (§4.2), that the natural MoE remedy collapses (§4.3), that the collapse cannot be rescued by standard MoE techniques (§4.4), and that the cause is normalization (§4.5)."* Even better: drop the roadmap entirely and let paragraph topic sentences carry the load.

**(R6) Lines 481-494, Observation 1.** Add a soft-motivation paragraph *before* the formal statement. SEMPO's pattern: 2 paragraphs of intuition, then one equation. You currently have **one** transitional sentence (line 479: "We now formalize it through an information-theoretic lens"). Expand to: a paragraph that walks through "what does the router need to see?" with no formalism, then a paragraph naming the three quantities $(M, \Sigma, S)$, then the Observation. Hedge "exact decomposition" → "an algebraic decomposition shows...".

**(R7) The four sub-claims (i)(ii)(iii)(iv) inside Observation 1 with the inline footnote.** Demote (iii) and (iv) to a corollary or to body prose. NeurIPS theorem environments contain ≤ 2 sub-clauses; (iv) is half a paragraph of empirical claims with a footnote — that does not belong inside a `\begin{observation}` block.

---

## Verdict

**The supervisor is right.** The technical content is NeurIPS-grade — the diagnosis is novel, the controls are dense, the cross-modal validation is appropriate. But the prose has *six* tech-report tells (bold-paragraph-headings, 8-numbers-per-sentence abstracts, contribution bullets that bury sub-claims, citation-clusters in opening sentences, roadmap-to-tables sectioning, theorem environments swallowing empirical claims) and the comparison papers have **none** of them. Both SRSNet and SEMPO let prose argue; your manuscript lets prose *log*. Tellingly: SRSNet's intro ends with three contribution bullets containing **zero numbers**; yours contains **>20**. The fix is mechanical, not conceptual — the science is there, the writing needs a structural pass focused on (a) deleting bold-paragraph-headings outside method sections, (b) moving numbers from intro/contributions/abstract into §4, and (c) inserting soft motivating prose before every formal block.
```

```
54	\begin{abstract}
55	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT and Moirai provide powerful pretrained representations, but adapting them to a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions. Standard TSFM benchmarks use a single static head---one adapter topology for every input window. A natural improvement is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter, where a router selects the best expert head for each window. However, on TSFMs with instance normalization, this \textbf{catastrophically fails}: the router learns to send \emph{every} window to the \emph{same} expert---routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$, and the remaining experts are never used. We identify \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse}: instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states that all look alike. Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---and all five standard MoE-rescue families (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) across eleven configurations fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism and yields a signal-ratio predictor ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) that identifies where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does \emph{not} (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$) on the primary backbone and generalizing across four additional backbones (two negative controls without instance normalization confirm specificity). A predicted consequence---the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}---is confirmed: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$, because unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse. A third architecture (\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}}) restoring raw-signal access at the expert level matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets (Appendix).
56	\end{abstract}

59	\label{sec:intro}
60	
61	{\looseness=-1 Time series foundation models (TSFMs)---MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, and others~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}---provide powerful pretrained representations, now scaling to billions of parameters with internal MoE routing. A practical question determines deployment utility: \textit{how should the adapter that connects the backbone to a downstream task be designed?}}
62	
63	\textbf{The problem with one-size-fits-all adapters.} Today, every public TSFM benchmark adapts the backbone with a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. But real time series are non-stationary---ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions---and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable expert.
64	
65	\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?} Frozen-backbone adaptation is compatible with established multi-tenant adapter deployment regimes~\citep{houlsby2019adapters,hu2022lora}---regimes that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot serve. A single TSFM in GPU VRAM can serve thousands of tenants via 426K-parameter adapters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB each) swapped in microseconds---eliminating $O(N)$ independent training pipelines. On-device deployment and cross-task reuse impose similar constraints (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes an increasingly important per-dataset adaptation path.
66	
67	\textbf{The collapse problem.} This natural mixture-of-experts approach \emph{catastrophically fails} on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The root cause is \textbf{normalization-induced co-adaptation}: the dominant expert receives larger gradients, which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, creating a feedback loop that collapses within ${\sim}50$ training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). Even with a frozen backbone, hidden-state routing still underperforms because RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish different input regimes. This is instance-normalization-specific: Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does \emph{not} collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}).
68	
69	\textbf{Our fix.} Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen. Only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. Eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) all fail to recover performance ($2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA across 720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), confirming that the problem is in the router's \emph{input}, not its \emph{optimization}.
70	
71	Our contributions are threefold:
72	
73	\textbf{(1)~A principle validated across three normalization families and two modalities: instance normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.} A mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) shows that instance normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics. The principle makes four \textbf{testable predictions}, all confirmed: (a)~$R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); (b)~backbones without instance normalization should not collapse (Timer-XL, Chronos; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}); (c)~cross-modality transfer (ViT$+$InstanceNorm1d collapses; ResNet does not; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); (d)~a phase-transition threshold $\alpha^* {=} R/(R{+}1) {\approx} 0.40$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition}, Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}). Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories: MOMENT collapses ($0.60{\to}0.00$) while Timer-XL \emph{rises} ($1.49{\to}1.60$)---same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
74	
75	\textbf{(2)~Fix and a predicted consequence.} Because the principle pinpoints the cause, the fix follows directly: RR-MoA routes on raw pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The principle also predicts a \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning---confirmed at $12$--$79\%$ across all six datasets. RR-MoA generalizes across four RevIN/LayerNorm backbones; two negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) confirm instance-normalization-specificity.
76	
77	\textbf{(3)~Actionable diagnosis.} The diagnosis is further validated by its predictive power: a third architecture, \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}), restores raw-signal access at the \emph{expert} level via a shared NLinear branch added to each expert's output. This closes the gap to supervised baselines, matching or beating DLinear on 6/6 datasets at $H{=}96$ ($107/123$ cells across six backbones; \S\ref{sec:main_results}).
78	
79	\section{Related Work}
80	
81	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
82	
83	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
```

```
477	\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: formal analysis.} The experimental evidence above converges on a clear mechanism, but relies on empirical observations. We now formalize it through an information-theoretic lens. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into three components: mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. RevIN maps $\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{S}_i$, discarding $(M_i, \Sigma_i)$. The following decomposition, while algebraically elementary (it follows from the MI chain rule), provides the formal basis for three testable quantitative predictions that we validate across nine datasets.
478	
479	\begin{observation}[Routing Information Loss Under Instance Normalization]
480	\label{thm:mi_decomp}
481	Let $X$ be a random input window, $E \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ the expert assignment produced by any deterministic router, and $S = (X - M)/\Sigma$ the RevIN-normalized shape.
482	\begin{enumerate}
483	    \item[\textup{(i)}] \textbf{Exact decomposition.} $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S) \geq 0$.
484	    \item[\textup{(ii)}] \textbf{Unconditional quantitative bound.} Without any independence assumption,
485	    \[
486	        I(X; E) - I(S; E) \;\geq\; I(M, \Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M, \Sigma;\, S),
487	    \]
488	    where the residual $\varepsilon := I(M, \Sigma;\, S) \geq 0$ measures the ``leakage'' of stripped statistics through the shape.  Equality (tightness) holds iff $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ given $E$.
489	    \item[\textup{(iii)}] \textbf{Full-information corner.} If the router depends \emph{entirely} on the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), then $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the \emph{entire} routing distribution in nats.
490	    \item[\textup{(iv)}] \textbf{Signal ratio as sufficient-statistic proxy.} Since Part~(iii) establishes that $(M,\Sigma)$ are sufficient statistics for $E$ when the router depends entirely on them, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ measures the variance contribution of these sufficient statistics relative to the residual shape---a monotone proxy for the \emph{potential} routing information in the stripped statistics. The leakage $\varepsilon$ varies by dataset ($0.09$--$1.26$ nats via CCA; cross-validated within ${\pm}0.2$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}); $R(\mathcal{D})$ is validated at $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ across nine datasets. \textbf{Tightness:} direct measurement of $H(E \mid S)$ via held-out classifier confirms normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy; the bound~(ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}).\footnote{$H(E \mid S)$ does not correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$); $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts improvement because it measures routing \emph{potential}, not the MI loss itself.}
491	\end{enumerate}
492	\end{observation}
493	
494	Full proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}; rate-distortion interpretation and phase-transition formalization in Appendix~\ref{app:prop2_depth}. \textit{Remark.} KSG cross-check (${\pm}0.26$ nats) confirms leakage estimates hold beyond Gaussianity. \textbf{Independent validation:} training $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as an \texttt{nn.Parameter}, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}).
495	
496	\textbf{Quantitative prediction.} The \emph{routing signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\text{Var}(M) + \text{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\text{Var}(S)}$ measures whether input windows in a dataset differ primarily in their location and scale (high $R$, normalization destroys the dominant routing signal) or primarily in their shape (low $R$, routing signal survives normalization). It serves as a monotone proxy for the MI bound. Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio} validates this: the Spearman rank correlation between $R(\mathcal{D})$ and the MSE improvement $\Delta\%$ from raw routing is $\rho = -0.88$ ($p < 0.002$; bootstrap CI: $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$), i.e., datasets where normalization strips more routing signal benefit more from bypassing it. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case ($\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$). Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier: the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+43\%$ degradation). Additional ablations (SSR, RDGF, per-quartile analysis) in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}.
```

```
54	
55	\begin{abstract}
56	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide powerful pretrained representations, but using them on a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head. A natural improvement over today's single-head designs is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter that selects a different head for each input window. We show that this natural design catastrophically fails on TSFMs with instance normalization: the router collapses to a single expert and the remaining experts are never used. The cause, which we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}, is that instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance the router needs to distinguish input regimes. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms---load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, and expert-choice---do not recover performance, because the failure is not in the router's optimization but in its input. We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition that yields a signal-ratio predictor of where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does not. The fix follows from the diagnosis: \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. RR-MoA wins on every dataset/freeze-level cell of the primary backbone, generalizes across four further backbones, and is confirmed to be instance-normalization-specific by two negative controls. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox} that we verify empirically: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse, so frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning. A companion architecture (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) restoring raw-signal access at the expert level closes the remaining gap to supervised baselines.
57	\end{abstract}
58	
59	\section{Introduction}
60	\label{sec:intro}
61	
62	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide powerful pretrained representations for time series, with several recent variants pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions, and the design of that adapter---more than the backbone choice---determines deployment utility.
63	
64	Today, every public TSFM benchmark uses a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. Real time series are not so uniform: ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions, and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical---one TSFM in GPU memory can serve thousands of tenants through small ($\sim$1.7\,MB) per-task adapters swapped in microseconds, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).
65	
66	This natural mixture-of-experts approach catastrophically fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to zero in most unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The router learns to send every window to the same expert, and the remaining experts are never used. The mechanism is what we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states. Even with the backbone frozen, hidden-state routing still underperforms; with the backbone unfrozen, the dominant expert receives larger gradients which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, closing a co-adaptation feedback loop within tens of training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). The failure is specific to instance normalization: backbones such as Moirai that use LayerNorm instead of RevIN do not collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). Standard MoE rescue mechanisms---load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice---also do not help (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), because the problem lies in the router's \emph{input}, not its optimization.
67	
68	Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is direct. \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen; only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning, which we confirm empirically.
69	
70	\paragraph{Contributions.}
71	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=0.15em, topsep=0.2em]
72	\item We identify \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}, a failure mode of MoE adapters on TSFMs that is distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE-rescue literature, and isolate it through eight converging causal controls.
73	\item We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) that yields a signal-ratio predictor of which datasets benefit from raw routing---including boundary cases where they do not---and validate the same principle across three normalization families, five backbones, and a vision modality.
74	\item We propose RR-MoA, a minimal architectural fix that routes on raw pre-normalization input, and a companion variant (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) that restores raw-signal access at the expert level. Together they close the gap to per-dataset supervised baselines while preserving frozen-backbone deployability.
75	\end{itemize}
76	
77	\section{Related Work}
78	
79	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
80	
81	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
82	
83	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.
84	
85	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental, and \citet{zou2025ibnorm} argue that variance-centric normalization (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) is suboptimal for representation learning because two representations with identical mean and variance can encode different amounts of task-relevant information. We identify a specific, mechanistic consequence of this principle that has not been characterized in the MoE literature: when the stripped statistics carry the \emph{routing} signal in a downstream MoE adapter, instance normalization causes catastrophic routing collapse---a failure mode distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE rescue literature.}
86	
87	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
```
