476	
477	\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: formal analysis.} The experiments above converge on a single mechanism: instance normalization strips the per-window statistics that the router uses to tell input regimes apart. To pin this down, we ask what information the router actually has access to before and after normalization. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into a mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, a scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and a shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. RevIN maps $\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{S}_i$ and discards $(M_i, \Sigma_i)$, so the question reduces to how much routing information lives in the discarded part. The mutual-information chain rule gives a clean answer.
478	
479	\begin{observation}[Routing Information Loss Under Instance Normalization]
480	\label{thm:mi_decomp}
481	Let $X$ be a random input window, $E \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ the expert assignment produced by any deterministic router, and $S = (X - M)/\Sigma$ the RevIN-normalized shape.
482	\begin{enumerate}
483	    \item[\textup{(i)}] \textbf{Exact decomposition.} $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S) \geq 0$.
484	    \item[\textup{(ii)}] \textbf{Quantitative bound.} Without any independence assumption,
485	    \[
486	        I(X; E) - I(S; E) \;\geq\; I(M, \Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M, \Sigma;\, S),
487	    \]
488	    where $\varepsilon := I(M, \Sigma;\, S) \geq 0$ captures any residual ``leakage'' of the stripped statistics through the shape. Equality holds iff $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ given $E$.
489	\end{enumerate}
490	\end{observation}
491	
492	Two limiting cases are worth naming. If the router's signal lies entirely in the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), the bound saturates and $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$---RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution in nats. At the opposite extreme, if $(M,\Sigma)$ carries no expert-relevant information, the loss is zero. Real datasets fall in between, with the loss bounded above by the variance the stripped statistics contribute to $X$. We therefore use the \emph{signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ as a tractable monotone proxy for how much potential routing information the stripped statistics could carry; it is not an estimate of the MI loss itself, but it is what we can compute on every dataset, and we use it to predict where raw routing will help. Full proof and a rate-distortion interpretation are in Appendices~\ref{app:proofs}, \ref{app:prop2_depth}.
493	
494	The bound is empirically tight on our datasets. Estimating the leakage with CCA gives $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated to within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}, so the result holds beyond Gaussianity. Direct measurement of $H(E \mid S)$ via a held-out classifier shows that normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of the routing entropy, and the bound (ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). As an independent check, training the normalization strength $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}). Notably, $H(E \mid S)$ alone does \emph{not} correlate with the empirical raw-routing benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$), while $R(\mathcal{D})$ does ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}): what matters is the routing \emph{potential} in the stripped statistics, not the MI loss.
495	
496	\textbf{Quantitative prediction.} The \emph{routing signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\text{Var}(M) + \text{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\text{Var}(S)}$ measures whether input windows in a dataset differ primarily in their location and scale (high $R$, normalization destroys the dominant routing signal) or primarily in their shape (low $R$, routing signal survives normalization). It serves as a monotone proxy for the MI bound. Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio} validates this: the Spearman rank correlation between $R(\mathcal{D})$ and the MSE improvement $\Delta\%$ from raw routing is $\rho = -0.88$ ($p < 0.002$; bootstrap CI: $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$), i.e., datasets where normalization strips more routing signal benefit more from bypassing it. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case ($\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$). Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier: the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+43\%$ degradation). Additional ablations (SSR, RDGF, per-quartile analysis) in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}.

**What now reads NeurIPS-grade:**

NeurIPS related-work sections often use them, so this one is **acceptable** — but the prose under each is dense and citation-packed. SRSNet's related work uses 2 lighter sub-headings. 4. **Conclusion** — I haven't reviewed it. If it's a numeric recap, it would benefit from the same treatment as the abstract. Worth a glance.

5. **The `\paragraph{Contributions.}` heading** — minor: NeurIPS papers sometimes drop the explicit "Contributions" label and let the bullets stand alone after a transition sentence. Either way is fine; SEMPO uses it, SRSNet doesn't.

**Verdict.** The supervisor's "this reads like a technical report" charge no longer applies to the abstract, intro, or theory block. 579	\section{Conclusion}
580	\vspace{-0.3em}
581	
582	We identified \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse} as the root cause of MoE adapter failure on time series foundation models. Eight causal controls---including opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast})---isolate the mechanism, and a mutual-information decomposition predicts where it applies ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{RR-MoA} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} and a Frozen Paradox where frozen adapters outperform full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. The diagnosis is further validated by its actionability: restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on $107/123$ cells across six backbones.
583	
584	\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Compute $R(\mathcal{D})$: in our 9 LTSF benchmarks, values above $0.5$ reliably predict raw routing helps (6/6 datasets, $27$--$77\%$ improvement). Below $0.2$ the prediction is one-sided: Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, $\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$) is correctly predicted to not benefit, but Solar ($R{=}0.06$, $\Delta{=}{-}32.9\%$) does benefit because the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale (SSR ablation, Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}). $R(\mathcal{D})$ thus captures a sufficient (not necessary) condition for raw routing to help; high $R$ is a strong positive predictor, while low $R$ does not rule out gains from richer temporal structure. \textbf{Limitations:} Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested; Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear backbones only (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers); $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses first moments and may miss higher-order routing signals (Solar outlier).

And the simplest possible fix---routing on the raw, pre-normalization input---wins consistently across datasets, freeze levels, backbones, and modalities. 578	\vspace{-0.5em}
579	\section{Conclusion}
580	\vspace{-0.3em}
581	
582	A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not work, and the reason is structural rather than algorithmic: the normalization layer the backbone relies on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics that a downstream router would have used to tell input regimes apart. Once that is recognized, every part of the empirical picture follows. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms cannot help, because they target the router's optimization rather than its input. Hidden-state routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones. Frozen-backbone adapters beat full fine-tuning, because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback. And the simplest possible fix---routing on the raw, pre-normalization input---wins consistently across datasets, freeze levels, backbones, and modalities. We see RR-MoA less as a new architecture than as the minimal architectural concession that the diagnosis forces.
583	
584	The diagnosis is also actionable: a tractable signal-ratio statistic computed on the raw data predicts which datasets benefit from raw routing without training any model, and the same principle generalises beyond MoE adapters to architectural choices like Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} that restore raw-signal access at the expert level.
585	
586	\textbf{Limitations.} Our analysis covers RevIN-style instance normalization and the five rescue families that dominate current MoE practice; whether other normalization schemes (e.g., the FFN-internal experts of Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe}) or yet-untried rescue mechanisms exhibit the same failure mode is open. The MI bound is exact, but the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses first and second moments only and can miss higher-order routing signals (Solar is the one such case in our suite). Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} is proved for linear backbones; the trajectory experiments confirm the mechanism in full Transformers but the formal extension is left to future work.
587

490	\end{observation}
491	
492	Two limiting cases are worth naming. If the router's signal lies entirely in the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), the bound saturates and $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$---RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution in nats. At the opposite extreme, if $(M,\Sigma)$ carries no expert-relevant information, the loss is zero. Real datasets fall in between, with the loss bounded above by the variance the stripped statistics contribute to $X$. We therefore use the \emph{signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ as a tractable monotone proxy for how much potential routing information the stripped statistics could carry; it is not an estimate of the MI loss itself, but it is what we can compute on every dataset, and we use it to predict where raw routing will help. Full proof and a rate-distortion interpretation are in Appendices~\ref{app:proofs}, \ref{app:prop2_depth}.
493	
494	The bound is empirically tight on our datasets. Estimating the leakage with CCA gives $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated to within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}, so the result holds beyond Gaussianity. Direct measurement of $H(E \mid S)$ via a held-out classifier shows that normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of the routing entropy, and the bound (ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). As an independent check, training the normalization strength $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}). Notably, $H(E \mid S)$ alone does \emph{not} correlate with the empirical raw-routing benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$), while $R(\mathcal{D})$ does ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}): what matters is the routing \emph{potential} in the stripped statistics, not the MI loss.
495	
496	Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio} reports the validation in detail. The Spearman rank correlation between $R(\mathcal{D})$ and the MSE improvement $\Delta\%$ from raw routing is $\rho = -0.88$ ($p < 0.002$; bootstrap CI $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$): datasets where normalization strips more routing signal benefit more from bypassing it. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case ($\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$). Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier; the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+43\%$ degradation). Additional ablations (SSR, RDGF, per-quartile analysis) are in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}.

we use it to predict where raw routing will help. Full proof and a rate-distortion interpretation are in
Appendices B, B.1.
The bound is empirically tight. CCA estimates ε ∈ [0.09, 1.26] nats, cross-validated to within ±0.26
nats by the KSG estimator [25]; a held-out classifier shows normalization retains only 16–41%
of the routing entropy and the bound (ii) gap averages 0.075 nats (4.7% of log K; Appendix L).
Independently, training the normalization strength α ∈ [0, 1] as a learnable parameter, gradient descent
converges to α < 0.5 on all six datasets (30/30 runs; Appendix K). The signal ratio R(D) predicts
the empirical raw-routing benefit at Spearman ρ=−0.88 (p<0.002; bootstrap CI [−1.00, −0.51];
n=9; Figure 5), while H(E | S) alone does not (ρ=−0.12): what matters for raw-routing benefit is
the routing potential in the stripped statistics, not the MI loss itself. Traffic (R=0.14, ∆=+2.9%) is
correctly predicted as a boundary case; Solar (R=0.06) is the one outlier, where the Conv1d router
exploits shape patterns beyond location-scale (SSR ablation: +43%; Appendix F).
Cross-backbone generalization. RR-MoA is not specific to MOMENT. On MOMENT-small and
MOMENT-large (both using RevIN), it wins all 21 configurations by 27–81% (Table O21). On
Moirai (LayerNorm only, no RevIN), it wins 18/18 by 3–31%—demonstrating that raw-signal routing
provides value beyond the RevIN diagnosis: even when hidden states retain enough information

Sparse routing and task generalization. Top-2 sparse routing adds 4.3 ms (+10%) while retaining
63% of the dense gain; scaling K=3→20 changes MSE by <5% (Appendix I). RR-MoA generalizes
to imputation (7/8 datasets; Appendix J).
Multi-horizon generalization. RR-MoA wins 24/24 configurations across H∈{96, 192, 336, 720}
on ETTh1, ETTm1, and Weather (5 seeds each; Table A1), with improvements of 27–49% over
the best fixed adapter at every horizon. The advantage is stable across horizon length: at H=720,
RR-MoA still improves by 27–41%. Residual-IA+ (Appendix R.1, Figure R5) further extends this to
all 6 datasets across 5 backbones and 4 horizons (Table R33).

5   Conclusion
A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not
work, and the reason is structural rather than algorithmic: the normalization layer the backbone relies
on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics that a downstream router would have used
to distinguish input regimes. Once that is recognized, the empirical picture follows. Standard MoE
rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot help; hidden-state
routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones; frozen
adapters beat full fine-tuning because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback; and the
simplest fix—routing on the raw, pre-normalization input—wins consistently across datasets, freeze
levels, backbones, and modalities. The diagnosis is also actionable: a tractable signal-ratio statistic
predicts which datasets benefit without training any model, and the same principle generalises beyond
MoE adapters to choices like Residual-IA+ that restore raw-signal access at the expert level. We see
RR-MoA less as a new architecture than as the minimal architectural concession the diagnosis forces.
Limitations. Our analysis covers RevIN-style instance normalization and the five rescue families
that dominate current MoE practice; whether other schemes (e.g., the FFN-internal experts of Time-
MoE [15]) exhibit the same failure mode is open. The signal ratio R(D) uses first and second
moments only and can miss higher-order routing signals (Solar in our suite). Proposition 1 is proved
for linear backbones; the trajectory experiments confirm the mechanism in full Transformers but the
formal extension is left to future work.

Proposition~\\ref{prop:frozen} is proved for linear backbones; the formal extension to full Transformers is left to future work."

Sparse routing, task and horizon generalization. Top-2 sparse routing retains most of the dense
gain at a +10% latency cost, and scaling K from 3 to 20 leaves MSE essentially unchanged (Ap-
pendix I). The advantage extends to imputation (7/8 datasets; Appendix J) and is stable across forecast
horizons H∈{96, 192, 336, 720} (24/24 wins at 27–49% over the best fixed adapter; Table A1). The
companion Residual-IA+ variant (Appendix R.1) extends this to all 6 datasets across 5 backbones
and 4 horizons (Table R33).

5   Conclusion
A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not
work, and the reason is structural: the normalization the backbone relies on for distribution shift also
strips the per-window statistics a downstream router needs to distinguish input regimes. Standard
MoE rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot help; hidden-
state routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones;
frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback;
the simplest fix—routing on the raw, pre-normalization input—wins consistently across datasets,
freeze levels, backbones, and modalities. The diagnosis is also actionable: a tractable signal-ratio
statistic predicts which datasets benefit without training any model, and the same principle generalises
beyond MoE adapters to choices like Residual-IA+ that restore raw-signal access at the expert level.
Limitations: our analysis covers RevIN-style instance normalization and the five dominant rescue
families; whether other schemes (e.g., Time-MoE [15]’s FFN-internal experts) exhibit the same
failure mode is open; R(D) uses second-order moments and can miss higher-order routing signals
(Solar in our suite); Proposition 1 is proved for linear backbones, with the formal extension to full
```

Cross-backbone generalization. RR-MoA is not specific to MOMENT. It wins all 21 MOMENT-
small and MOMENT-large configurations (27–81%; Table O21) and 18/18 Moirai configurations
(3–31%), the latter showing that raw-signal routing helps even on LayerNorm-only backbones whose
hidden states already retain routing information. On Moirai-MoE [12], which already contains sparse
internal experts, RR-MoA still improves all 6 datasets by 37–90% (Table O22): adapter-level and
backbone-internal routing operate on complementary axes. The two negative controls predicted by
Observation 1—Chronos and Timer-XL [10], neither of which uses instance normalization—show
no collapse and no RR-MoA gain (4/18 wins, within chance; Appendix O).

\newlabel{fig:framework}{{1}{3}{\textbf {RR-MoA architecture.} \textit {Path~A} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$ (no gradients through $\theta $); all experts receive $\mathbf {H}$. \textit {Path~B} (orange): a lightweight Conv1d gate (1{,}100 params) reads the raw pre-normalization signal $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ and selects the Top-2 experts via sparse routing. Only the selected experts (bold) contribute to the output; inactive experts (gray) receive no gradient. Standard MoE routing on $\mathbf {H}$ collapses (entropy $0.000{\pm }0.000$; Table~\ref {tab:adamix}); RR-MoA achieves \textbf {54/54 wins} (Table~\ref {tab:rrmoa})}{figure.1}{}}
\newlabel{fig:trajectory}{{2}{6}{\textbf {Per-step routing / gradient trajectory} (AdaMix, ETTh1). (a)~Unfrozen+RevIN (red) collapses within ${\sim }50$ steps; strictly frozen control (blue) stays stable, isolating gradient co-adaptation from optimizer or data effects. (b)~Dominant expert's gradient grows while others starve (co-adaptation loop, \S \ref {sec:rrmoa}). Removing RevIN (separate experiment, Figure~\ref {fig:causal_contrast}) shows the trajectory inverts}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:causal_contrast}{{3}{7}{\textbf {Causal contrast: MOMENT vs Timer-XL} (ETTh1, last-4 unfreezing). MOMENT entropy collapses $0.51{\to }0.000$ in ${\sim }40$ steps (red); Timer-XL stays at ${\approx }1.60$ for all $400$ steps (orange). Same code, same data, only normalization differs. Pattern generalizes across all 3 tested datasets}{figure.3}{}}
\newlabel{fig:dose_response}{{4}{9}{\textbf {Normalization dose-response} (frozen, 5 seeds $\times $ 6 datasets). \textbf {Left:} MSE vs $\alpha $ ($0{=}$raw, $1{=}$RevIN). Phase transition at $\alpha {=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), mild for $\alpha {\leq }0.75$ ($+5.4\%$). \textbf {Right:} entropy stays high at all $\alpha $---normalization renders routing uninformative, not collapsed}{figure.4}{}}
\newlabel{fig:frozen_paradox}{{5}{9}{\textbf {Left: Frozen Paradox}---frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by $12$--$79\%$. \textbf {Right: Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho {=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases}{figure.5}{}}
\newlabel{fig:signal_ratio}{{5}{9}{\textbf {Left: Frozen Paradox}---frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by $12$--$79\%$. \textbf {Right: Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho {=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases}{figure.5}{}}
\newlabel{fig:routing_appendix}{{E1}{19}{\textbf {Multi-seed RR-MoA routing weights per dataset} (Top-2 sparse, strictly frozen, mean$\pm $std over seeds $\{42,43,44\}$). Routing is diverse and dataset-dependent: ETTh1 spreads weight roughly uniformly (entropy $1.495\pm 0.034$); ETTm1 concentrates on Last+Max; Weather on Mean+Conv1d}{figure.1}{}}
\newlabel{fig:collapse_mechanism}{{F2}{19}{\textbf {Normalization-induced routing collapse mechanism.} \textit {Left:} Raw input windows with distinct characteristics (amplitude, trend, volatility) are routed to different experts. \textit {Right:} After instance normalization strips $\mu $ and $\sigma $, all windows become indistinguishable, and the router collapses to a single expert (entropy $\to 0.000$)}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:srmoa_arch}{{F3}{20}{\textbf {SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma _k$ reading $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly---no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf {H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph {raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref {fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle---not the specific router---drives the gains}{figure.3}{}}
\newlabel{fig:routing_viz}{{F4}{20}{\textbf {Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips---empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma ) \perp \!\!\!\perp S$ from Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp}(iii)}{figure.4}{}}
\newlabel{fig:residual_ia_arch}{{R5}{27}{\textbf {Residual-IA\textsuperscript {+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit {Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit {Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf {y}_\mathrm {raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf {y}_k = \mathbf {y}_\mathrm {raw} + \sigma (\mathrm {blend}_k(\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw})) \cdot \mathrm {Adapter}_k(\mathbf {H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma $ gates (orange) on $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf {6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf {107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times $ 6 datasets $\times $ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref {tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref {tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb})}{figure.5}{}}

492	Two limiting cases pin down the bound. If the router's signal lives entirely in the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), the bound saturates and $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$---RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution. If $(M,\Sigma)$ carries no expert-relevant information, the loss is zero. Real datasets fall in between, and the loss is bounded by the variance the stripped statistics contribute to $X$. We therefore use the \emph{signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ as a tractable monotone proxy for that variance contribution---computable on every dataset, used to predict where raw routing will help. Full proof in Appendices~\ref{app:proofs}, \ref{app:prop2_depth}.
493	
494	The bound is empirically tight: CCA gives $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by KSG~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}; a held-out classifier shows normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of the routing entropy with bound (ii) gap averaging $0.075$ nats (Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). Training $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}). $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts the raw-routing benefit at Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}), while $H(E \mid S)$ alone does not ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$): routing \emph{potential} in the stripped statistics matters, not the MI loss itself. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, $\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case; Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier (SSR ablation $+43\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).

5   Conclusion
A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not
work, and the reason is structural: the normalization the backbone relies on for distribution shift also
strips the per-window statistics a downstream router needs to distinguish input regimes. Standard
MoE rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot help; hidden-
state routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones;
frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback;
the simplest fix—routing on the raw, pre-normalization input—wins consistently across datasets,
freeze levels, backbones, and modalities. The diagnosis is also actionable: a tractable signal-ratio
statistic predicts which datasets benefit without training any model, and the same principle generalises
beyond MoE adapters to choices like Residual-IA+ that restore raw-signal access at the expert level.
Limitations: our analysis covers RevIN-style instance normalization and the five dominant rescue
families; whether other schemes (e.g., Time-MoE [15]’s FFN-internal experts) exhibit the same
failure mode is open; R(D) uses second-order moments and can miss higher-order routing signals
(Solar in our suite); Proposition 1 is proved for linear backbones, with the formal extension to full
Transformers left to future work.

References
 [1] Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez,

5   Conclusion
A natural MoE adapter on instance-normalized time series foundation models fails for structural
reasons: the normalization the backbone relies on for distribution shift also strips the per-window
statistics a downstream router needs. Once recognized, the empirical picture follows—rescue
mechanisms targeting the router’s optimization cannot help, hidden-state routing collapses only on
instance-normalized backbones, frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning, and routing on the raw pre-
normalization input wins across datasets, freeze levels, backbones, and modalities. The signal-ratio
statistic predicts where the fix helps without training, and the same principle motivates Residual-IA+ ,
which restores raw-signal access at the expert level. Limitations: our analysis covers RevIN-style
instance normalization and the five dominant rescue families; R(D) uses second-order moments
and can miss higher-order signals (Solar); Proposition 1 is proved for linear backbones, with the
Transformer extension left to future work.

5   Conclusion
A natural MoE adapter on instance-normalized time series foundation models fails for structural
reasons: the normalization the backbone relies on for distribution shift also strips the per-window
statistics a downstream router needs. Once recognized, the empirical picture follows—rescue
mechanisms targeting the router’s optimization cannot help, hidden-state routing collapses only on
instance-normalized backbones, frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning, and routing on the raw pre-
normalization input wins across datasets, freeze levels, backbones, and modalities. The signal-ratio
statistic predicts where the fix helps without training, and the same principle motivates Residual-IA+ ,
which restores raw-signal access at the expert level. Limitations: our analysis covers RevIN-style
instance normalization and the five dominant rescue families; R(D) uses second-order moments
and can miss higher-order signals (Solar); Proposition 1 is proved for linear backbones, with the
Transformer extension left to future work.

References

Figure 5: Left: Frozen Paradox—frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by 12–79%. Right: Observation 1

                     (i) Exact decomposition. I(X; E) − I(S; E) = I(M, Σ; E | S) ≥ 0.
              (ii) Quantitative bound. Without any independence assumption,
                                                    I(X; E) − I(S; E) ≥ I(M, Σ; E) − I(M, Σ; S),
                          where ε := I(M, Σ; S) ≥ 0 captures any residual “leakage” of the stripped statistics
                          through the shape. Equality holds iff (M, Σ) ⊥⊥ S given E.
In the limit where the router’s signal lives entirely in the stripped statistics (E ⊥⊥ S | (M, Σ)), the
bound saturates and I(X; E) − I(S; E) = H(E)—RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution.
We therefore use the signal ratio R(D) = [Var(M ) + Var(Σ)]/Var(S) as a tractable monotone
proxy for the variance contribution of the stripped statistics. The bound is empirically tight: CCA
gives ε ∈ [0.09, 1.26] nats, cross-validated within ±0.26 nats by KSG [25]; a held-out classifier
shows normalization retains only 16–41% of routing entropy with bound (ii) gap averaging 0.075 nats
(Appendix L). Training α ∈ [0, 1] as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to α < 0.5
on all six datasets (30/30 runs; Appendix K). R(D) predicts the raw-routing benefit at Spearman
ρ=−0.88 (p<0.002, n=9; Figure 5); H(E | S) alone does not (ρ=−0.12), since routing potential
in the stripped statistics matters, not the MI loss itself. Traffic (R=0.14, ∆=+2.9%) is correctly
predicted as a boundary case; Solar (R=0.06) is the one outlier (SSR ablation +43%; Appendix F).

477	\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: formal analysis.} The experiments above converge on a single mechanism: instance normalization strips the per-window statistics that the router uses to tell input regimes apart. To pin this down, we ask what information the router actually has access to before and after normalization. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into a mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, a scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and a shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. RevIN maps $\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{S}_i$ and discards $(M_i, \Sigma_i)$, so the question reduces to how much routing information lives in the discarded part. The mutual-information chain rule gives a clean answer.

5   Conclusion
A natural MoE adapter on instance-normalized TSFMs fails for structural reasons: the normalization
the backbone relies on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics a downstream router
needs. Standard rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot
help; routing on the raw, pre-normalization input does, and the same principle predicts the Frozen
Paradox and motivates Residual-IA+ . The signal-ratio statistic identifies where the fix applies without
training. Limitations: we cover RevIN-style normalization and the five dominant rescue families;
R(D) uses second-order moments and can miss higher-order signals (Solar); Proposition 1 is proved
for linear backbones, with the Transformer extension left to future work.

References
 [1] Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez,
```

The sharpness of the transition arises from the softmax: when $P_\mathrm{route}(\alpha) / P_\mathrm{noise}$ drops below ${\sim}1$, routing weights converge to uniform regardless of expert relevance.

945	\textbf{Information bottleneck connection.}
946	The RevIN-encoder pipeline implements a form of the information bottleneck~\citep{tishby2000ib}: it compresses $X$ into a representation $H = f_\theta(S)$ that is optimized for downstream prediction while discarding ``irrelevant'' variability (the per-window location-scale statistics). The routing MI loss from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) is the price paid for this compression \emph{at the routing decision point}. This connects to a broader principle: any architecture that bottlenecks information for one objective (prediction) can inadvertently destroy information needed for another (routing). The vision cross-modality control (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) confirms this is not RevIN-specific: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patches creates the same bottleneck, while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does not---because spatial features are not the routing signal for classification.

 \maketitle
 
 \begin{abstract}
-Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT and Moirai provide powerful pretrained representations, but adapting them to a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions. Standard TSFM benchmarks use a single static head---one adapter topology for every input window. A natural improvement is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter, where a router selects the best expert head for each window. However, on TSFMs with instance normalization, this \textbf{catastrophically fails}: the router learns to send \emph{every} window to the \emph{same} expert---routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$, and the remaining experts are never used. We identify \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse}: instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states that all look alike. Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---and all five standard MoE-rescue families (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) across eleven configurations fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism and yields a signal-ratio predictor ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) that identifies where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does \emph{not} (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$) on the primary backbone and generalizing across four additional backbones (two negative controls without instance normalization confirm specificity). A predicted consequence---the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}---is confirmed: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$, because unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse. A third architecture (\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}}) restoring raw-signal access at the expert level matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets (Appendix).
+Time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide powerful pretrained representations, but using them on a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head. A natural improvement over today's single-head designs is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter that selects a different head for each input window. We show that this natural design catastrophically fails on TSFMs with instance normalization: the router collapses to a single expert and the remaining experts are never used. The cause, which we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}, is that instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance the router needs to distinguish input regimes. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms---load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, and expert-choice---do not recover performance, because the failure is not in the router's optimization but in its input. We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition that yields a signal-ratio predictor of where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does not. The fix follows from the diagnosis: \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. RR-MoA wins on every dataset/freeze-level cell of the primary backbone, generalizes across four further backbones, and is confirmed to be instance-normalization-specific by two negative controls. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox} that we verify empirically: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse, so frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning. A companion architecture (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) restoring raw-signal access at the expert level closes the remaining gap to supervised baselines.
 \end{abstract}
 
 \section{Introduction}
 \label{sec:intro}
 
-{\looseness=-1 Time series foundation models (TSFMs)---MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, and others~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}---provide powerful pretrained representations, now scaling to billions of parameters with internal MoE routing. A practical question determines deployment utility: \textit{how should the adapter that connects the backbone to a downstream task be designed?}}
+Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide powerful pretrained representations for time series, with several recent variants pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions, and the design of that adapter---more than the backbone choice---determines deployment utility.
 
-\textbf{The problem with one-size-fits-all adapters.} Today, every public TSFM benchmark adapts the backbone with a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. But real time series are non-stationary---ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions---and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable expert.
+Today, every public TSFM benchmark uses a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. Real time series are not so uniform: ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions, and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical---one TSFM in GPU memory can serve thousands of tenants through small ($\sim$1.7\,MB) per-task adapters swapped in microseconds, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).
 
-\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?} Frozen-backbone adaptation is compatible with established multi-tenant adapter deployment regimes~\citep{houlsby2019adapters,hu2022lora}---regimes that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot serve. A single TSFM in GPU VRAM can serve thousands of tenants via 426K-parameter adapters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB each) swapped in microseconds---eliminating $O(N)$ independent training pipelines. On-device deployment and cross-task reuse impose similar constraints (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes an increasingly important per-dataset adaptation path.
+This natural mixture-of-experts approach catastrophically fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to zero in most unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The router learns to send every window to the same expert, and the remaining experts are never used. The mechanism is what we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states. Even with the backbone frozen, hidden-state routing still underperforms; with the backbone unfrozen, the dominant expert receives larger gradients which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, closing a co-adaptation feedback loop within tens of training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). The failure is specific to instance normalization: backbones such as Moirai that use LayerNorm instead of RevIN do not collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). Standard MoE rescue mechanisms---load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice---also do not help (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), because the problem lies in the router's \emph{input}, not its optimization.
 
-\textbf{The collapse problem.} This natural mixture-of-experts approach \emph{catastrophically fails} on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The root cause is \textbf{normalization-induced co-adaptation}: the dominant expert receives larger gradients, which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, creating a feedback loop that collapses within ${\sim}50$ training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). Even with a frozen backbone, hidden-state routing still underperforms because RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish different input regimes. This is instance-normalization-specific: Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does \emph{not} collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}).
+Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is direct. \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen; only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning, which we confirm empirically.
 
-\textbf{Our fix.} Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen. Only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. Eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) all fail to recover performance ($2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA across 720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), confirming that the problem is in the router's \emph{input}, not its \emph{optimization}.
-
-Our contributions are threefold:
-
-\textbf{(1)~A principle validated across three normalization families and two modalities: instance normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.} A mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) shows that instance normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics. The principle makes four \textbf{testable predictions}, all confirmed: (a)~$R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); (b)~backbones without instance normalization should not collapse (Timer-XL, Chronos; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}); (c)~cross-modality transfer (ViT$+$InstanceNorm1d collapses; ResNet does not; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); (d)~a phase-transition threshold $\alpha^* {=} R/(R{+}1) {\approx} 0.40$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition}, Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}). Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories: MOMENT collapses ($0.60{\to}0.00$) while Timer-XL \emph{rises} ($1.49{\to}1.60$)---same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
-
-\textbf{(2)~Fix and a predicted consequence.} Because the principle pinpoints the cause, the fix follows directly: RR-MoA routes on raw pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The principle also predicts a \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning---confirmed at $12$--$79\%$ across all six datasets. RR-MoA generalizes across four RevIN/LayerNorm backbones; two negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) confirm instance-normalization-specificity.
-
-\textbf{(3)~Actionable diagnosis.} The diagnosis is further validated by its predictive power: a third architecture, \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}), restores raw-signal access at the \emph{expert} level via a shared NLinear branch added to each expert's output. This closes the gap to supervised baselines, matching or beating DLinear on 6/6 datasets at $H{=}96$ ($107/123$ cells across six backbones; \S\ref{sec:main_results}).
+\paragraph{Contributions.}
+\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=0.15em, topsep=0.2em]
+\item We identify \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}, a failure mode of MoE adapters on TSFMs that is distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE-rescue literature, and isolate it through eight converging causal controls.
+\item We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) that yields a signal-ratio predictor of which datasets benefit from raw routing---including boundary cases where they do not---and validate the same principle across three normalization families, five backbones, and a vision modality.
+\item We propose RR-MoA, a minimal architectural fix that routes on raw pre-normalization input, and a companion variant (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) that restores raw-signal access at the expert level. Together they close the gap to per-dataset supervised baselines while preserving frozen-backbone deployability.
+\end{itemize}
 
 \section{Related Work}
 
-\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
+\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment} are the canonical choices. A recent line of work has explored variations on this theme: multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, and PEFT alternatives surveyed for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}. Related benchmarking and model-selection work includes TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval}. What unifies these efforts is that they search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---while keeping a single adapter architecture. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should itself be chosen per input window.
 
-\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
+\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been used \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale capacity, with experts placed inside the backbone architecture: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes are complementary rather than competing: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
 
 \textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.

use gemini nano banana pro to visualise the problem: "Time series foundation models like MOMENT and Moirai are powerful pretrained
representations. But the standard way to adapt them is to attach a single static head — one
adapter topology for every input window, no matter what the data looks like.
A natural improvement is mixture-of-expert adapters: a pool of structurally diverse heads with a
learned router that picks the best expert per window. AdaMix and Switch Transformer have
shown this works well in NLP.
Here is where things go sideways. On TSFMs that use instance normalization — and most of
the major ones do — this standard MoE recipe catastrophically fails. Routing entropy
collapses to exactly 0.000 in 7 of 12 unfrozen configurations. The router learns to send
every single sample to the same expert. The other four experts are dead weight.
Our first instinct was: this is a known optimization issue. So we tried all five standard rescue
families from the MoE literature — load balancing from Switch, z-loss from ST-MoE, entropy
regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice. Eleven configurations across a 720-run sweep.
Zero of eleven recover. Still 2.7× worse than what we’ll show next.
Our claim — and the rest of this talk defends it — is that the MoE field has been treating this as
an optimization problem. We show it’s actually an information problem"

I have all the info needed. Here are the verbatim facts from the doc:

**Model ID for Nano Banana Pro:** `gemini-3-pro-image-preview`

**API key env var:** `GEMINI_API_KEY` (used in HTTP header `x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY`; the `genai.Client()` picks it up automatically)

**Aspect ratios supported:** `"1:1","1:4","1:8","2:3","3:2","3:4","4:1","4:3","4:5","5:4","8:1","9:16","16:9","21:9"`
**Image sizes (resolution):** `"512", "1K", "2K", "4K"`

**Verbatim Python snippet (basic text-to-image, from doc):**

```python
from google import genai
from google.genai import types
from PIL import Image

client = genai.Client()

prompt = ("Create a picture of a nano banana dish in a fancy restaurant with a Gemini theme")
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview",
    contents=[prompt],
)

for part in response.parts:
    if part.text is not None:
        print(part.text)
    elif part.inline_data is not None:
        image = part.as_image()
        image.save("generated_image.png")
```

**Verbatim aspect-ratio + resolution config (Python, from doc) — applies to `gemini-3-pro-image-preview`:**

```python
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview",  # swap to "gemini-3-pro-image-preview"
    contents=[prompt],
    config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
        image_config=types.ImageConfig(
            aspect_ratio="16:9",
            image_size="2K",
        )
    )
)
```

Doc explicitly states this `image_config` form (with both `aspect_ratio` and `image_size`) is the form for `gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview` and `gemini-3-pro-image-preview`. For `gemini-2.5-flash-image`, only `aspect_ratio` is supported (no `image_size`).

{
  "file_path": "/Users/hungpq2412/.claude/skills/gemini-academic-viz/SKILL.md",
  "content": "---\nname: gemini-academic-viz\ndescription: Generate publication-quality academic figures and conceptual diagrams using Google's Gemini 3 Pro Image (Nano Banana Pro). Use this skill whenever the user wants to create a figure, diagram, illustration, or conceptual visualization for a paper, presentation, slide deck, blog post, or talk — especially for ML/AI research, scientific concepts, system architectures, or methodology overviews. Trigger this skill for phrases like \"make a figure\", \"visualize this concept\", \"create a diagram\", \"generate an academic illustration\", \"Nano Banana\", \"Gemini image\", \"image for the paper\", \"figure for my talk\", \"draw this for me\", or whenever the user describes a phenomenon they want a polished visual of. Prefer this skill over freehand prompting because it bakes in the prompt patterns and API parameters that have been verified to produce paper-grade (not infographic-y) output.\n---\n\n# Gemini Academic Visualization\n\nGenerate publication-grade figures with Google's Gemini 3 Pro Image model (codename \"Nano Banana Pro\"). The model is excellent at scientific diagrams, architectural figures, two-panel comparisons, and conceptual illustrations — but only if the prompt is specifically engineered to suppress its default \"slide-deck infographic\" tendencies and produce something that would pass for a NeurIPS / ICML / Nature paper figure.\n\n## When to use\n\n- The user wants a figure for a paper, talk, slide, or blog post.\n- The user wants to visualize a concept, mechanism, architecture, or failure mode.\n- The user mentions \"Nano Banana\", \"Gemini image\", \"image generation\", or names a Google image model.\n- The user has a verbal description of a phenomenon and wants it rendered as a clean diagram.\n\nDo **not** use this skill for: photo editing, logo design, marketing creative, or generation tasks where the user explicitly asked for a different model (DALL-E, Midjourney, etc.).\n\n## Pre-flight checks\n\n1. Locate `GEMINI_API_KEY` in the project's `.env` (or in environment). If missing, ask the user before proceeding.\n2. Confirm the working Python env has `google-genai` and `Pillow` installed:\n   ```bash\n   python3 -c \"import google.genai, PIL\" 2>&1\n   ```\n   If the import fails, install: `pip install google-genai Pillow`.\n3. Pick an output directory under the project (default: `figures/talk/` or `figures/generated/`).\n\n## Workflow\n\nThe proven workflow is **prompt → run the bundled script → view → iterate**.\n\n1. **Engineer the prompt** following `references/prompt_style.md`. The single most important thing is to lock the style explicitly: paper-figure look, not slide / infographic / 3D / glossy. The user's request will usually describe *what* to draw — your job is to wrap it in the academic-style scaffolding.\n2. **Save the prompt + name in `scripts/generate.py`** (or call it via the CLI — see below). Run it. The script handles the API call, aspect ratio, resolution, and saving the PNG.\n3. **View the result** by reading the saved PNG with the Read tool — it renders inline.\n4. **Iterate** on the prompt if the result is off. Common failure modes and fixes are in `references/prompt_style.md`.\n\nAim for first-shot quality — each generation costs ~30–60s of wall time and a non-trivial API call. Spend the time getting the prompt right rather than spamming attempts.\n\n## Bundled script\n\n`scripts/generate.py` is a self-contained generator. Two ways to use it:\n\n**Inline (recommended for one-offs):** edit the `PROMPTS` dict in the file or pass via CLI flag:\n```bash\npython3 ~/.claude/skills/gemini-academic-viz/scripts/generate.py \\\n    --name problem_overview \\\n    --out figures/talk/problem_overview.png \\\n    --prompt \"$(cat <<'EOF'\n<your full academic-styled prompt here>\nEOF\n)\"\n```\n\n**Programmatic:** import and call `generate(name, prompt, out_path, aspect=\"16:9\", size=\"2K\")` from another script.\n\nDefaults: aspect `16:9`, size `2K`, model `gemini-3-pro-image-preview`. Override aspect to `1:1` for square figures, `3:2` for portrait-ish papers, `9:16` for posters.\n\n## Model and API parameters\n\n- **Model ID:** `gemini-3-pro-image-preview` (Gemini 3 Pro Image, aka Nano Banana Pro). Use this for academic figures — it has higher fidelity than `gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview` (Nano Banana 2 Flash) and renders text labels far more legibly.\n- **Aspect ratios supported:** `1:1, 1:4, 1:8, 2:3, 3:2, 3:4, 4:1, 4:3, 4:5, 5:4, 8:1, 9:16, 16:9, 21:9`.\n- **Image sizes:** `512`, `1K`, `2K`, `4K`. Default to `2K` for paper figures (crisp text, reasonable file size).\n- **Auth:** API key in `GEMINI_API_KEY` env var. The `genai.Client()` constructor picks it up automatically.\n\n## What good looks like\n\nA successful academic figure from this skill:\n- Renders all label text legibly without typos (Pro is good at this; Flash is not).\n- Uses a restrained palette: white background + at most 2–3 accent colors.\n- Has clean vector-style strokes, no drop shadows, no gradients, no 3D extrusion.\n- Composes panels with explicit `(a)`, `(b)` labels and short banner headlines that the model renders verbatim.\n- Conveys the *mechanism* rather than just the topic — e.g., shows three distinct waveforms entering normalization and emerging homogenized, not just a generic \"TSFM diagram\".\n\nIf the output looks like a marketing infographic, a slide deck graphic, or a children's textbook illustration, the prompt didn't push hard enough on the academic-style anti-prompts. See `references/prompt_style.md` for what to add.\n\n## Reference files\n\n- `references/prompt_style.md` — The academic prompt style guide: positive cues, anti-prompts, multi-panel composition pattern, common failure modes, and a worked example.\n"
}

  "content": "# Academic Prompt Style Guide\n\nGemini 3 Pro Image has a strong default toward \"slide-deck infographic\" output: glossy, 3D-tilted, drop-shadowed, marketing-bright. The job of the prompt is to suppress those defaults and aim the model at a NeurIPS / ICML / Nature look.\n\n## The five dials\n\nEvery academic prompt should explicitly set these five dials. Skipping any of them lets the model regress to its defaults.\n\n1. **Genre lock.** Say what kind of artifact this is: *\"a publication-quality figure for a NeurIPS submission\"*, *\"a Nature-style methods diagram\"*, *\"a black-and-white textbook figure\"*. Don't say \"slide\" or \"presentation\" unless that's literally what you want — those words pull toward infographic territory.\n2. **Negative style list.** Spell out what to avoid: *\"not a slide, not infographic, not 3D, not glossy, no drop shadows, no gradients, no decorative emoji, no logo\"*. This is non-negotiable for paper figures.\n3. **Color discipline.** Specify the palette explicitly. Default: *\"white background, monochrome navy blue lines, at most one or two muted accent colors (e.g., orange for highlights), light gray for inactive elements\"*. Avoid asking for more than three accent colors — academic figures rarely use them.\n4. **Typography.** Specify *\"clean sans-serif typography (Helvetica, Inter, or similar)\"* and *\"all text labels must be perfectly legible\"*. The Pro model renders text well; explicit clarity prompts make it sharper.\n5. **Strokes and shapes.** Specify *\"thin vector-style strokes, sharp corners or gently rounded boxes, no shadows, no extrusion\"*.\n\n## Composition patterns that work\n\n### Two-panel comparison (status quo vs. failure mode)\n\nThis is the strongest pattern for a paper's headline figure. Layout:\n\n```\nPANEL A (top, labeled '(a) <short descriptor>'):\n  <one-sentence banner headline that should appear verbatim above panel A>\n  <left-to-right pipeline drawn as boxes + arrows>\n\nPANEL B (bottom, labeled '(b) <short descriptor>'):\n  <same architecture but with the change/failure highlighted>\n  <one-sentence banner headline verbatim above panel B>\n\nVisual style: <the five dials from above>\nAspect 16:9, single composed figure, thin horizontal divider between panels.\n```\n\nWhy it works: the model is good at reusing the shared architecture across both panels, and the explicit `(a) (b)` labeling forces a clean composition. The verbatim banner headlines render reliably with Pro.\n\n### Single architecture diagram\n\n```\nA clean, paper-figure-style architecture diagram of <system>.\nComposition (left to right):\n  - <input nodes: describe shape, what they are>\n  - <processing block: name, sub-label>\n  - <intermediate state: what it represents>\n  - <output / decision node>\nAnnotate <key elements> with <small labels>.\nVisual style: <the five dials>.\nAspect <ratio>, single figure, no panels.\n```\n\n### Mechanism-revealing diagram (what we did for routing collapse)\n\nThe trick: don't just draw the system. Draw *the moment the mechanism does its work*. For routing collapse, the figure had three visually-distinct waveforms entering instance normalization and *emerging visually identical* on the other side — the figure shows the stripping, not just the architecture. For an attention diagram, you might show the same input attended-to under two different masking patterns, side by side. For a generalization-failure diagram, show the train and test distributions with the train cluster filled and the test cluster hollow.\n\nAlways describe *what changes* across the diagram, not just *what is there*.\n\n## Negative prompts (paste these verbatim)\n\nThe exact phrase that worked in practice for the RR-MoA problem-overview figure:\n\n> *\"Visual style: monochrome scientific figure with minimal accent colors --- white background, navy blue lines for the architecture, muted orange only for the active expert in panel B and for highlighting key terms, light gray for dimmed/inactive components. Sans-serif typography (similar to Helvetica or Inter), thin vector-style strokes, NeurIPS / ICML paper-figure look (not a slide, not infographic, not 3D, not glossy). All text labels must be perfectly legible, no decorative emoji, no shadows, no gradients.\"*\n\nIf you keep this paragraph in every prompt you send, you'll be 80% of the way to academic style.\n\n## Common failure modes and fixes\n\n| Symptom | Cause | Fix |\n|---|---|---|\n| Looks like a marketing slide | Forgot the negative prompts | Add the negative-prompt paragraph above. |\n| Has 3D depth / shadows | \"Editorial illustration\" or \"infographic\" leaked into the prompt | Replace with \"paper figure\" or \"scientific diagram\". |\n| Random emoji in corners | Default decoration | Add *\"no decorative emoji, no logo, no watermark\"*. |\n| Text is blurry or misspelled | Used Flash, not Pro | Switch model to `gemini-3-pro-image-preview`. |\n| Six bright colors everywhere | Palette under-specified | Specify exactly which colors and what they encode. |\n| Wrong number of items (e.g., 4 experts instead of 5) | Count buried in a long sentence | State counts up front and repeat: *\"five expert heads (E1, E2, E3, E4, E5)\"*. |\n| Headline banner text mangled | Pro generally gets it right, but long banners can fail | Keep banner headlines under ~14 words; quote them with surrounding markers like \"reads in clean sans serif:\". |\n| Components labeled wrong | Names not anchored to their visual element | Phrase as *\"box labeled 'X'\"* or *\"node tagged 'X'\"* rather than just naming things in passing. |\n\n## Worked example\n\nThe successful RR-MoA problem-overview prompt — keep this as a template:\n\n> *An academic-paper-quality scientific figure for a NeurIPS submission, rendered as a clean two-panel diagram comparing the standard practice (panel A) with its natural extension that catastrophically fails (panel B). The two panels share the same underlying architecture so the reader can see exactly what changes.*\n>\n> *PANEL A (top, labeled '(a) Standard practice: one static head'): A horizontal pipeline drawn left-to-right. On the left, three distinct univariate time-series input windows of length 512 are stacked vertically, each rendered as a small inline waveform plot in a thin gray frame: window 1 is a smooth slow sinusoid, window 2 is a noisy high-volatility signal, window 3 is a sharp step pattern. Each window feeds into the same large rounded box labeled 'Frozen TSFM Backbone (e.g., MOMENT, Moirai)' with a small lock icon, and a tiny tag underneath reading 'Instance Normalization (RevIN)'. The backbone produces hidden states H, drawn as a stack of three small matrices, which all flow into ONE single head box labeled 'Single static adapter head'. The head's output is labelled y_hat. Only E1 is drawn in solid orange, with a thick bold orange arrow from the router into E1. E2 through E5 are drawn faded in gray, with thin dashed inactive arrows and a small label 'unused' next to each. To the right of the expert column a small inline annotation reads 'routing entropy = 0.000'. A header banner above panel B reads in clean sans serif: 'A natural mixture-of-experts adapter catastrophically collapses on instance-normalized TSFMs'.*\n>\n> *Visual style: monochrome scientific figure with minimal accent colors --- white background, navy blue lines for the architecture, muted orange only for the active expert in panel B and for highlighting key terms, light gray for dimmed/inactive components. Sans-serif typography (similar to Helvetica or Inter), thin vector-style strokes, NeurIPS / ICML paper-figure look (not a slide, not infographic, not 3D, not glossy). All text labels must be perfectly legible, no decorative emoji, no shadows, no gradients. 16:9 aspect ratio, single composed figure, panels stacked vertically with a thin horizontal divider line between them.*\n\nNotice the structure: opening genre lock, panel A description with banner headline, panel B description with banner headline, closing visual-style paragraph. Use this skeleton; swap the content.\n\n## Output sizes and aspect ratios\n\nPick by destination:\n\n- Paper headline figure: `16:9, 2K`\n- Paper square figure (e.g., a scatter or a 1-panel mechanism): `1:1, 2K`\n- Talk slide: `16:9, 2K`\n- Poster panel: `9:16, 2K` or `2:3, 4K`\n- Inline schematic: `3:2, 1K`\n\n`4K` is rarely needed for figures that will be embedded in a PDF — it just makes files large.   "content": "\"\"\"Generate an academic-quality figure with Gemini 3 Pro Image (Nano Banana Pro).\n\nDesigned for the gemini-academic-viz skill. Two usage modes:\n\n1) CLI for one-off generations:\n   python3 generate.py --name myfig --out figures/myfig.png \\\n       --prompt \"$(cat prompt.txt)\" --aspect 16:9 --size 2K\n\n2) Programmatic from another Python file:\n   from generate import generate\n   generate(\"myfig\", PROMPT_TEXT, \"out.png\", aspect=\"16:9\", size=\"2K\")\n\nReads GEMINI_API_KEY from a `.env` in the working directory or from the\nprocess environment. The Gemini SDK's Client() picks it up automatically.\n\"\"\"\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nimport argparse\nimport os\nimport sys\nfrom pathlib import Path\nfrom typing import Optional\n\n\ndef load_env(path: Path) -> None:\n    \"\"\"Minimal .env loader. Existing env vars take precedence.\"\"\"\n    if not path.exists():\n        return\n    for line in path.read_text().splitlines():\n        line = line.strip()\n        if not line or line.startswith(\"#\") or \"=\" not in line:\n            continue\n        k, v = line.split(\"=\", 1)\n        os.environ.setdefault(k.strip(), v.strip().strip('\"').strip(\"'\"))\n\n\ndef generate(\n    name: str,\n    prompt: str,\n    out_path: str | Path,\n    aspect: str = \"16:9\",\n    size: str = \"2K\",\n    model: str = \"gemini-3-pro-image-preview\",\n) -> Path:\n    \"\"\"Call Nano Banana Pro and save the resulting PNG.\n\n    Returns the path written. Raises on API failure or empty response.\n    \"\"\"\n    from google import genai\n    from google.genai import types\n\n    out_path = Path(out_path)\n    out_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n\n    if not os.environ.get(\"GEMINI_API_KEY\"):\n        raise RuntimeError(\n            \"GEMINI_API_KEY is not set. Add it to .env or export it before calling.\"\n        )\n\n    client = genai.Client()\n    print(f\"[gemini-viz] {name}: requesting {model} ({aspect}, {size})...\", flush=True)\n\n    response = client.models.generate_content(\n        model=model,\n        contents=[prompt],\n        config=types.GenerateContentConfig(\n            image_config=types.ImageConfig(\n                aspect_ratio=aspect,\n                image_size=size,\n            )\n        ),\n    )\n\n    saved = False\n    for part in response.parts:\n        text = getattr(part, \"text\", None)\n        if text:\n            # The model sometimes includes a brief textual description alongside\n            # the image. Surface it for debugging but don't fail.\n            print(f\"[gemini-viz] {name}: model text -> {text[:200]}\", flush=True)\n        if getattr(part, \"inline_data\", None):\n            img = part.as_image()\n            img.save(out_path)\n            print(\n                f\"[gemini-viz] {name}: saved {out_path} ({out_path.stat().st_size} bytes)\",\n                flush=True,\n            )\n            saved = True\n            break\n\n    if not saved:\n        raise RuntimeError(\n            f\"No image data returned for prompt '{name}'. Check the prompt or try a \"\n            \"different aspect ratio / size.\"\n        )\n    return out_path\n\n\ndef main() -> int:\n    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)\n    p.add_argument(\"--name\", required=True, help=\"Short name for logging.\")\n    p.add_argument(\"--out\", required=True, help=\"Output PNG path.\")\n    p.add_argument(\"--prompt\", help=\"Prompt text. If omitted, reads stdin.\")\n    p.add_argument(\"--prompt-file\", help=\"Path to a file containing the prompt.\")\n    p.add_argument(\"--aspect\", default=\"16:9\", help=\"Aspect ratio (default 16:9).\")\n    p.add_argument(\"--size\", default=\"2K\", help=\"Image size: 512, 1K, 2K, 4K (default 2K).\")\n    p.add_argument(\n        \"--model\",\n        default=\"gemini-3-pro-image-preview\",\n        help=\"Model ID (default gemini-3-pro-image-preview).\",\n    )\n    p.add_argument(\"--env-file\", default=\".env\", help=\"Path to .env file (default ./.env).\")\n    args = p.parse_args()\n\n    load_env(Path(args.env_file))\n\n    if args.prompt:\n        prompt = args.prompt\n    elif args.prompt_file:\n        prompt = Path(args.prompt_file).read_text()\n    else:\n        prompt = sys.stdin.read()\n\n    if not prompt.strip():\n        print(\"error: empty prompt\", file=sys.stderr)\n        return 2\n\n    try:\n        generate(\n            name=args.name,\n            prompt=prompt,\n            out_path=args.out,\n            aspect=args.aspect,\n            size=args.size,\n            model=args.model,\n        )\n    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001\n        print(f\"[gemini-viz] FAILED -- {type(e).__name__}: {e}\", file=sys.stderr)\n        return 1\n    return 0\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    sys.exit(main())\n"

209	\subsection{Problem Formulation and Expert Pool}
210	
211	For a mixture of adapters to be effective, the expert pool must contain structurally diverse heads so that the router has meaningful choices. An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. We maintain $K{=}5$ topologically distinct expert adapters (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool), identified from structural motifs across ${\sim}1{,}200$ architectures in an LLM-guided search (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}). Architectural diversity is critical: replacing the five distinct heads with five identical experts (same topology, different initialization) degrades MSE by $8$--$15\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
212	
213	\textbf{Standard protocol.} Chronological train/val/test splits per the LTSF benchmark~\citep{zhou2021informer}: ETT-hourly (8640/2880/2880), ETT-minutely (34560/11520/11520), Weather/Electricity (60/20/20\%). Final evaluation uses the held-out test set.
214	
215	\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
216	\label{sec:rrmoa}
217	
218	The goal of per-window routing is to select, for each input window, the subset of expert adapters best suited to that window's characteristics---so that a quiet baseline and a volatile spike are handled by different adapter topologies rather than forced through the same head. As shown in the introduction, this fails when the router reads normalized hidden states, because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:
