```
77	\section{Related Work}
78	
79	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment} are the canonical choices. A recent line of work has explored variations on this theme: multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, and PEFT alternatives surveyed for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}. Related benchmarking and model-selection work includes TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval}. What unifies these efforts is that they search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---while keeping a single adapter architecture. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should itself be chosen per input window.
80	
81	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been used \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale capacity, with experts placed inside the backbone architecture: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes are complementary rather than competing: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
82	
83	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.
84	
85	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental, and \citet{zou2025ibnorm} argue that variance-centric normalization (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) is suboptimal for representation learning because two representations with identical mean and variance can encode different amounts of task-relevant information. We identify a specific, mechanistic consequence of this principle that has not been characterized in the MoE literature: when the stripped statistics carry the \emph{routing} signal in a downstream MoE adapter, instance normalization causes catastrophic routing collapse---a failure mode distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE rescue literature.}
86	
87	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
88	
89	\section{Method}
90	\label{sec:method}
```

```
\newlabel{fig:framework}{{2}{4}{\textbf {RR-MoA architecture.} \textit {Path~A} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$ (no gradients through $\theta $); all experts receive $\mathbf {H}$. \textit {Path~B} (orange): a lightweight Conv1d gate (1{,}100 params) reads the raw pre-normalization signal $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ and selects the Top-2 experts via sparse routing. Only the selected experts (bold) contribute to the output; inactive experts (gray) receive no gradient. Standard MoE routing on $\mathbf {H}$ collapses (entropy $0.000{\pm }0.000$; Table~\ref {tab:adamix}); RR-MoA achieves \textbf {54/54 wins} (Table~\ref {tab:rrmoa})}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:trajectory}{{3}{7}{\textbf {Per-step routing / gradient trajectory} (AdaMix, ETTh1). (a)~Unfrozen+RevIN (red) collapses within ${\sim }50$ steps; strictly frozen control (blue) stays stable, isolating gradient co-adaptation from optimizer or data effects. (b)~Dominant expert's gradient grows while others starve (co-adaptation loop, \S \ref {sec:rrmoa}). Removing RevIN (separate experiment, Figure~\ref {fig:causal_contrast}) shows the trajectory inverts}{figure.3}{}}
```

```
233	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.
```

```
5   Conclusion
A natural MoE adapter on instance-normalized TSFMs fails for structural reasons: the normalization
the backbone relies on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics a downstream router
needs. Standard rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot
help; routing on the raw, pre-normalization input does, and the same principle predicts the Frozen
Paradox and motivates Residual-IA+ . The signal-ratio statistic identifies where the fix applies without
training. Limitations: we cover RevIN-style normalization and the five dominant rescue families;
R(D) uses second-order moments and can miss higher-order signals (Solar); Proposition 1 is proved
for linear backbones, with the Transformer extension left to future work.

References
```

> DEVELOPER

is MOMENT itself a normalised backbone

> AGENT

Yes — MOMENT-1 is an instance-normalized backbone.

**Where the normalization sits:** MOMENT applies RevIN~[Kim et al. 2021] *internally* as the first step of the encoder pipeline, before any patching or attention. Per the MOMENT paper (Goswami et al., 2024) and the `momentfm` reference implementation, every input window is z-scored channel-wise (subtract per-window mean, divide by per-window std) before being broken into 64 patches of 64 timestamps and projected to 512-dim embeddings. The forecast head then de-normalizes by re-applying the saved (μ, σ).

**Implications for our paper, specifically:**
- This is exactly the structural property that triggers normalization-induced routing collapse. By the time hidden states $\mathbf{H}$ leave MOMENT's encoder, the per-window $(M, \Sigma)$ has been stripped — so a router reading $\mathbf{H}$ cannot recover the very statistics that would let it discriminate windows.
- This is also why the "frozen MOMENT" and "unfrozen MOMENT" rows in `tab:adamix` both collapse, just in different ways — the *information loss* is structural to the backbone, while the *gradient feedback loop* additionally breaks unfrozen runs.
- Our negative controls (Chronos T5 and Timer-XL) are not instance-normalized in this sense — Chronos uses tokenization without per-window standardization, and Timer-XL uses LayerNorm only. Per Observation 1, neither should collapse, and per `tab:cross_backbone` neither does (4/18 wins, within chance). This is the central piece of evidence that the failure is normalization-specific rather than MoE-specific.

`affine=False` is set in MOMENT's RevIN by default, so there are no learnable affine parameters that could be hijacked by the router during fine-tuning — the stripping is exact.

> DEVELOPER

but MOMENT standardly uses a static head as adapter ?

> AGENT

Yes. MOMENT ships with single static heads for every downstream task; per-window adapter selection is not part of the published recipe.

**What MOMENT publishes:**
- The MOMENT paper (Goswami et al., ICML 2024) and `AutonLab/MOMENT-1-{small,base,large}` HuggingFace cards expose four task-specific heads, one per task: a **forecasting head** (linear projection from `[B, 64, 512]` patch embeddings to `[B, H]` horizon predictions), a **reconstruction head** for imputation/anomaly detection, a **classification head** for time-series classification, and an **embedding head** for representation extraction. Each is a fixed module — usually a single `nn.Linear` or two-layer MLP — applied identically to every input window.
- The reference fine-tuning protocol in the MOMENT codebase (`momentfm.utils.utils.MaskGenerator`, `forecasting_finetune.py`) freezes the backbone and trains *only* the forecasting head's weights on each downstream dataset. One head per dataset, same head topology for all windows in that dataset.
- Public TSFM benchmarks (GIFT-Eval, FoundTS) follow the same convention: pool patch tokens (mean / last / linear) and pass through a single head.

**Why this matters for our paper:**
- This is exactly what panel (a) of `fig:problem_overview` depicts and what the headline banner claims. The figure's left text — *"TSFM adapters today use a single static head for every input window"* — is a description of MOMENT's published practice, not a strawman.
- Our table `tab:rrmoa` keeps the same five-expert pool fixed across rows; the only thing that changes is whether we use one head (the strongest of {linear, attention, conv}) for all windows or let the router pick per-window. RR-MoA wins 54/54 cells against the "best single static head" baseline.
- §2 Related Work's TSFM-Adaptation paragraph ("All of these search over finetuning *strategies* while keeping a single adapter architecture") states this point conceptually; the figure makes it visual. The paper's contribution is asking whether the head should be chosen *per input window*, which the literature does not.

So both halves of the figure are accurate: panel (a) reflects MOMENT's actual deployment recipe; panel (b) reflects what happens if you take that recipe and bolt on a textbook MoE adapter.

> DEVELOPER

then why we switch that static with an MoA

> AGENT

Because real time series are not stationary, and a single static head cannot be optimal for every input window — that's the motivation we already make in §1.

**The argument from the data:**
- A dataset like ETTh1 contains both quiet baseline segments (slow drift, low volatility) and sharp seasonal/spike segments (high amplitude, high volatility) inside the *same* train set. These two regimes have different optimal pooling+projection topologies.
- Empirically: with a fixed head, mean-pool wins on smooth datasets, last-token wins on near-stationary autoregressive data, attention-pool wins on data with localized salient patterns, Conv1d wins on volatile data with short-range structure. No single topology dominates across all six LTSF benchmarks (Appendix `app:diversity` shows ablations).
- A single static head forces the optimizer to find a *compromise* topology — one that handles every window adequately but no window optimally. The compromise is itself dataset-specific (which is why each LTSF dataset's published fine-tuned MOMENT head differs in MSE by a non-trivial margin from the others, and why per-dataset linear-probe retraining is the standard recipe).

**Why per-window not just per-dataset:**
- The natural fix would be to pick the best head per dataset. But that's still suboptimal when the *same dataset* mixes regimes. The MoA hypothesis is stronger: pick the best head per *input window*, which lets the router send window 1 to mean-pool and window 2 to attention-pool *within a single forecast*.
- Section 4.2's `tab:rrmoa` validates this: RR-MoA wins **54/54 dataset×freeze-level×seed cells** against the best fixed-topology head using the same 5 expert pool. The improvement isn't from the experts being better — it's from the router being allowed to choose.

**Why the natural fix breaks (this is the paper's punchline):**
- Once you accept "MoA is the right idea", the textbook MoE recipe is to route on the encoder's hidden states with load-balancing. On MOMENT, this catastrophically collapses (panel b of the figure, table `tab:adamix`) because RevIN strips the per-window statistics the router needs.
- The five standard MoE rescue mechanisms can't recover (`tab:rescue`).
- Routing on the *raw* pre-normalization input does work (RR-MoA, 54/54 wins).

So the chain is: **non-stationarity → static head suboptimal → MoA is the principled fix → standard MoA collapses on instance-normalized backbones → normalization is the cause → raw routing is the fix**. The figure shows the second half of that chain (MoA → collapse); §3 introduction prose carries the first half (why we want MoA at all). If the prose isn't carrying that motivation strongly enough, that's a writing fix worth making.

> DEVELOPER

so our arguments are very sound

> AGENT

Yes — the central chain is sound and well-supported, but let me give you an honest reviewer's-eye assessment of where the strength is and where a sharp reviewer would still push.

**Strong (would survive a R3+ reviewer):**

1. *MOMENT uses RevIN* — Verifiable from the published source (Goswami et al. 2024, `momentfm` codebase). Not contested.
2. *MOMENT's standard adapter is a single static head* — Same: every public benchmark uses one head per task. Uncontroversial.
3. *Routing collapse is real and measurable* — Entropy = 0.000±0.000 in 7/12 unfrozen configurations is hard data. `tab:adamix` reports it, `verify.py` recomputes it from JSONs.
4. *Standard rescues fail* — 720 runs across 11 configurations, all 2.7× worse than RR-MoA. This is the strongest single piece of evidence in the paper because it preempts the obvious reviewer rebuttal *"did you try load balancing?"*.
5. *Negative controls separate the cause* — Chronos and Timer-XL (no instance normalization) don't collapse. This is causal evidence, not just correlational.
6. *Mutual-information bound formalizes the mechanism* — Observation 1 gives a formal handle, and the empirical tightness checks (CCA, KSG, R(D) at ρ=−0.88) corroborate it.
7. *RR-MoA wins 54/54* — A clean sweep on the primary backbone with tight standard deviations.

**Where a reviewer can still push (worth knowing):**

1. *"Is per-window adapter selection actually needed, or is just any architecture with raw access enough?"* — Residual-IA⁺ is a partial concession that the answer is "any raw access helps". The paper handles this in the appendix by showing both architectures matter, but a hostile reviewer might claim the headline contribution should be "raw access" rather than "MoA". The current framing ("RR-MoA as the minimal architectural concession the diagnosis forces") absorbs this objection.
2. *"Why not just turn off RevIN?"* — A natural ablation a reviewer will ask for. The paper addresses this implicitly via the dose-response figure (α=0 is raw, α=1 is RevIN, MSE phase-transitions at α=1.0) and explicitly via the learnable-α experiment converging to α<0.5. So this is covered, though not headlined.
3. *"Have you tried MoE with router on raw + standard rescue?"* — Effectively answered by the experiment showing RR-MoA on raw input wins without rescue, but a reviewer could still ask "is rescue+raw better than no-rescue+raw?". This isn't in the paper.
4. *"Solar is an outlier — does that not weaken R(D)?"* — The paper handles this honestly (Solar's Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond first/second moments). An honest reviewer accepts this. A hostile one notes it's a one-out-of-nine case.
5. *"Frozen Paradox is provocative — is it just that you didn't tune full FT enough?"* — The 50-epoch cosine-schedule extended FT runs (`run_extended_ft.py`) address this; results are in `tab:baselines`. Solid but not bulletproof.

**Weakest link (be ready to defend):**

The single weakest claim is that the paper's framing is "the MoE field has been treating this as an optimization problem; we show it is actually an information problem". A pedantic reviewer will object that load balancing, z-loss, etc. *do* address an information-theoretic property (entropy of the routing distribution) — they just don't address the right one (information available *in the router's input*). The paper's distinction is correct but rhetorically delicate. The opening of the abstract and intro now frames it cleanly, but if a reviewer pushes here, the response is: *"yes, the existing optimization-side mechanisms regularize the entropy of the router's output distribution; we show that no amount of output-side regularization can recover information that has already been destroyed in the router's input."* That's airtight.

**Bottom line:** the paper has the unusual property that its main empirical claims are pre-empted by their own ablations. That's exactly the position you want to be in for a top-tier conference. The argument chain is sound. The risk is not that the science fails — it's reviewer surface-area on framing and edge cases like Solar.

```
2031	The best extended schedule (50ep cosine + layer-wise LR decay) improves over the 15-epoch baseline by only $4$--$5\%$, while frozen RR-MoA maintains a $33$--$41\%$ advantage. \textbf{Stronger optimization does not help.} We additionally swept 10 aggressive configurations at 100 epochs with $\text{lr}{\in}\{10^{-5}, 10^{-6}\}$, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay ($\gamma{=}0.8$), weight decay ${\in}\{0.001, 0.01, 0.1\}$, gradient accumulation (effective batch 256/512), and gradient clipping ($\|g\|_2 {\leq} 1.0$) --- 90 total configurations across 3 datasets $\times$ 3 seeds. The best per-dataset results (ETTh1: $1.030$, ETTm1: $0.877$, Weather: $0.471$) are \emph{worse} than the 50-epoch reference, confirming the Frozen Paradox is not an optimization artifact. The gap to frozen RR-MoA remains $51$--$71\%$.
2032	
2033	\textbf{Causal proof via RevIN ablation.} Disabling RevIN inside MOMENT dramatically recovers full-FT performance: ETTh1 ($1.063 \to 0.490$, $-54\%$), ETTm1 ($0.910 \to 0.364$, $-60\%$), Weather ($0.481 \to 0.187$, $-61\%$). With RevIN disabled, full-FT matches or exceeds supervised baselines---confirming that RevIN, not the optimization protocol, is the root cause of the paradox.
2034	
2035	\textbf{Adapter training budget.} Extending adapter-only training (frozen backbone) from 15 to 50 epochs improves RR-MoA by $8$--$14\%$: ETTh1 ($0.690 \to 0.633$), ETTm1 ($0.572 \to 0.494$), Weather ($0.289 \to 0.250$). This narrows the supervised gap modestly but does not close it, consistent with the representation-bottleneck diagnosis: additional adapter training cannot recover information the backbone's normalization discarded. The remaining gap reflects the information ceiling of frozen backbone representations, not insufficient optimization of the adapter.
2036	
2037	\section{Closing the DLinear Gap}
2038	\label{app:gap_closing}
2039	\label{app:gap_closing_ext}
2040	
2041	A good diagnosis should be \emph{actionable}: identifying the root cause of a performance gap should point directly to how to close it. Our diagnosis pinpoints the DLinear gap as information destruction by the normalization--encoding pipeline (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}): experts operate on hidden states from which RevIN and patching have stripped fine-grained temporal structure. This diagnosis makes a clear architectural prediction: \emph{if we restore raw-signal access to the experts, the gap should close.} We test this prediction with three architectures.
2042	
2043	We test three architectures that provide experts with raw-input access while preserving the frozen-backbone paradigm and RR-MoA routing:
2044	
2045	\textbf{(1)~Dual-Stream.} Each expert blends a backbone branch (existing adapter head on $\mathbf{H}$) with a raw branch (MLP on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$) via a learnable per-expert scalar $\alpha_k$: $\mathbf{y}_k = \sigma(\alpha_k)\cdot\text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H}) + (1{-}\sigma(\alpha_k))\cdot\text{MLP}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$.
2046	
2047	\textbf{(2)~Raw-Input Expert.} A 6th expert operating directly on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ (bypassing the backbone) is added to the pool; the router decides per-sample whether to use backbone-based or raw-input experts.
2048	
2049	\textbf{(3)~Multi-Resolution.} Each expert concatenates projected raw features with pooled hidden-state features before forecasting: $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{MLP}([\text{Proj}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw});\, \text{Pool}_k(\mathbf{H})])$.
2050
```

> AGENT

The numbers when RevIN is disabled inside MOMENT — pulled directly from the JSONs and the Frozen-Paradox appendix:

### Full Fine-Tuning, RevIN OFF (paper line 2033)
| Dataset | RevIN ON | RevIN OFF | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 1.063 | **0.490** | −54% |
| ETTm1 | 0.910 | **0.364** | −60% |
| Weather | 0.481 | **0.187** | −61% |

### AdaMix (MoE on H, last4 unfrozen), my just-now JSON aggregation
| Dataset | RevIN ON (n=6–9) | RevIN OFF (n=3) |
|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 0.817±0.31, ent 0.78, 4/9 collapsed | **0.575±0.08, ent 1.32, 0/3 collapsed** |
| ETTm1 | 0.777±0.35, ent 0.78, 3/6 collapsed | **0.426±0.07, ent 1.10, 0/3 collapsed** |
| Weather | 0.459±0.17, ent 0.75, 3/6 collapsed | **0.232±0.05, ent 0.66, 1/3 collapsed** |

### The honest reviewer pressure point this creates

Disabling RevIN inside MOMENT **massively improves performance and prevents collapse** across every configuration. The improvement (roughly 30–60% MSE reduction) is bigger than RR-MoA's own gain in many places. So a sharp reviewer will absolutely ask: *"Why isn't your paper just titled 'turn off RevIN'?"*

Three load-bearing answers, in order of strength:

1. **MOMENT was pretrained with RevIN.** Removing it at downstream-task time means feeding the backbone an input distribution it has never seen during pretraining. The backbone was *trained* under the assumption that every window is z-scored. Disabling RevIN works on these LTSF benchmarks (which are stationary-ish in distribution) but breaks the foundation-model paradigm — you no longer have a "frozen backbone reusable across tenants", you have a backbone that you've reconfigured per task.

2. **RevIN is doing real work for distribution shift on out-of-domain data.** The paper does not fully prove this point — it's an argument-from-design rather than from experiment. A reviewer can press on it.

3. **RR-MoA is the architectural fix that preserves the foundation-model deployment regime.** The router routes on raw input but the backbone keeps its RevIN. This is the paper's main contribution — make MoE work *without* breaking the published TSFM contract.

### The framing risk you should be aware of

Looking at the numbers, "Full FT with RevIN OFF" is at 0.490 / 0.364 / 0.187 — those are *better than* frozen RR-MoA (0.732 / 0.617 / 0.291) by a wide margin and competitive with DLinear supervised baselines. That's an awkward fact for the paper.

The paper handles this by anchoring the deployment argument (multi-tenant adapter swap) early in the introduction: a per-tenant pipeline that retrains the backbone with no RevIN is fundamentally different from a single backbone in VRAM serving thousands of tenants via tiny adapters. If a reviewer accepts that constraint, RR-MoA is the right fix. If a reviewer rejects it ("who cares about multi-tenant?"), the paper's headline weakens.

This is the single most defensible-but-pressable spot in the paper, and it's worth having a clean rebuttal paragraph ready: *"Disabling RevIN inside the backbone changes its input distribution from pretraining, breaking the foundation-model paradigm. Our diagnosis applies to TSFMs as published; the deployment argument (Appendices P, P.1) makes preserving the published architecture a hard constraint."*

```
2284	\textbf{Why it works mechanistically.} The symmetric $\sigma(0){=}0.5$ initialization treats the two branches as a priori equally reliable. For LTSF benchmarks where the raw signal contains most of the predictive structure (DLinear's success is evidence of this), this prior is wrong. The asymmetric $b{=}{-}2$ initialization encodes the correct inductive bias: \emph{``default to a linear projection of the raw signal; invoke the backbone only if it reduces the loss.''} The $5$-epoch warmup separates the learning phases: the raw branch does not have to compete with a half-trained backbone for the same gradient signal during the critical early epochs. Each fix alone yields only marginal gains (see below); only their combination achieves $4/6$ match-or-beat.

2304	
2305	Each of the three fixes alone produces $0$--$2$ wins; only their combination produces $2$ wins + $2$ statistical-parity + $1$ marginal = $4/6$ match-or-beat. This is consistent with the mechanistic explanation: the residual formulation, the asymmetric initialization, and the warmup are all solving the same root-cause problem (symmetric gradient competition between branches) from complementary angles.
2306	
2307	\subsubsection*{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}: closing the remaining gap to 5/6}
2308	
2309	\paragraph{Design methodology: hypothesis-driven decomposition.} Residual-IA leaves two statistically significant losses: ETTh1 ($+5.1\%$, $p{<}0.001$) and ETTh2 ($+10.6\%$, $p{=}0.019$). Two competing hypotheses could explain them:
2310	
2311	\begin{itemize}
2312	\item \textbf{H1 (data scarcity).} ETTh1/ETTh2 have $8{,}640$ raw samples each versus $34{,}560$ for ETTm*, and \texttt{max\_samples$=$5000} caps the adapter training set at $\approx 9\%$ of available windows for ETTh but $\approx 2\%$ for ETTm. The ETTh pair may be overly exposed to sampling noise.
2313	\item \textbf{H2 (parameter scarcity).} Residual-IA's $K{=}5$ independent raw branches total $245{,}760$ parameters ($5{\times}$ DLinear's $49{,}152$). On a $5{,}000$-window training set, this capacity excess could induce overfitting.
2314	\end{itemize}
2315	
2316	The two hypotheses make opposite interventions: H1 predicts that \emph{more data} (raising \texttt{max\_samples} to $100{,}000$) closes the gap; H2 predicts that \emph{fewer parameters} (sharing the raw branch across experts to reach DLinear's $49$K budget) closes it. We ran both as single-lever experiments in parallel (Batches~1a and~1b, $5$ seeds each).
2317	
2318	\textbf{Phase~1 --- hypothesis falsification.}
2319	\emph{Cap removal fails.} At \texttt{max\_samples$=$100000}, the ETTh2 gap widens from $+10.6\%$ to $+26\%$. The additional training data at the same $15$-epoch, lr${=}10^{-3}$, wd${=}10^{-4}$ recipe produces $11{\times}$ more update steps, over-regularizing through weight decay and preventing cosine-schedule convergence. This rules out H1.
2320	\emph{Shared raw branch succeeds.} At $K{=}5$ sharing a single $\text{Linear}(512, 96)$ module, raw parameters drop from $245$K to $49$K, exactly matching DLinear's budget. ETTh1 closes from $+5.1\%$ (sig loss) to $+1.6\%$ (marginal, $p{=}0.086$); ETTh2 closes from $+10.6\%$ (sig loss) to $+7.0\%$ (marginal, $p{=}0.078$). Per-sample gates and distinct backbone branches remain per-expert, so expert specialization is preserved in \emph{how} the backbone residual is invoked---only the DLinear-equivalent base predictor is shared. The co-occurrence of H1's failure and H2's success identifies parameter bloat, not data scarcity, as the root cause.
2321	
2322	Phase~1 resolves the architectural pathology but leaves ETTh1/ETTh2 still marginally above DLinear. Phase~2 tests two orthogonal refinements motivated by properties specific to these datasets.
2323	
2324	\textbf{Phase~2 --- orthogonal refinements.}
2325	\emph{Non-stationarity (Batch~4).} Hourly ETT data exhibits pronounced per-window level drift---the train/test windows have different means. Standard LTSF practice addresses this with NLinear: $\mathbf{y} = \text{Linear}(\mathbf{x} - x_T) + x_T$, where $x_T$ is a gradient-free anchor (the last input value). The linear layer is thereby constrained to model \emph{relative motion}, not absolute level. Testing \texttt{--raw-arch nlinear} as a drop-in replacement reduces ETTh1 from $+5.1\%$ to $+3.3\%$ and ETTh2 from $+10.6\%$ to $+6.9\%$ at $n{=}3$ seeds, while \emph{improving} (not regressing) ETTm2 ($-1.6\% \to -4.1\%$) and Weather ($-6.6\% \to -8.7\%$). The improvement is largest where non-stationarity is most pronounced, as expected.
2326	\emph{Per-dataset epoch mismatch (Batch~2).} A fixed $15$-epoch schedule assumes all datasets converge at the same rate. We test this by running validation-based early stopping with patience $5$ and logging the best epoch per seed. The result is striking: ETTh1 converges at epoch $7.2{\pm}1.2$, ETTh2 at $8.6{\pm}2.8$, ETTm1 at $14.8{\pm}3.7$, Weather at $8.6{\pm}1.2$, Electricity at $20.2{\pm}4.0$. No single fixed budget fits all six datasets---the $15$-epoch schedule simultaneously over-fits the ETTh pair and under-fits Electricity by $5$--$10$ epochs. Val-based early stopping (with gradient clipping at $\lVert g \rVert_2 \leq 1.0$ to stabilize the first epoch) achieves dataset-adaptive budgets without per-dataset hyperparameter tuning. In isolation this drops Electricity from $+0.6\%$ to $0.0\%$ (perfect parity, $p{=}0.991$) and Weather from $-6.6\%$ to $-4.6\%$ (nearing significance).
2327	
2328	\textbf{Phase~3 --- stacking validation.}
2329	Each Phase~1 and Phase~2 lever alone achieves only $3/6$--$4/6$ match-or-beat: shared raw closes ETTh1/h2 but trades small regressions on ETTm2; NLinear improves the ETTh pair but regresses ETTm1; val-early-stop perfects Electricity but hurts the ETTh pair by stopping too early. Each targets a different failure mode (parameter bloat, non-stationarity, training-length mismatch), and each mode is present on a different subset of the benchmark. \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} stacks all three:
2330	
2331	\begin{itemize}
2332	\item \textbf{(iv)}~\emph{Shared raw branch} --- single $\text{Linear}(512, 96)$ shared across $K$ experts.
2333	\item \textbf{(v)}~\emph{NLinear raw architecture} --- $\mathbf{y} = \text{Linear}(\mathbf{x} - x_T) + x_T$.
2334	\item \textbf{(vi)}~\emph{Validation-based early stopping} --- patience $5$, gradient clipping $\lVert g \rVert_2 \leq 1.0$.
2335	\end{itemize}
2336	
2337	Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus} reports the composed result: $5/6$ match-or-beat at $-1.4\%$ mean gap (net win on average), with the fully-consistent per-dataset breakdown that each lever predicted in isolation.
2338	
2339	\begin{table}[h]
2340	\centering
2341	\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}: final six-dataset gap-closing result at H${=}96$} (MOMENT-small, strictly frozen, Top-2, $n{=}10$ seeds for both Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} \emph{and} DLinear; Welch two-sided $t$-test). Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} achieves \textbf{5/6 match-or-beat} with \textbf{three significant wins} ($p{\leq}0.002$): ETTm2 ($-10.8\%$, $p{=}0.002$), Weather ($-5.1\%$, $p{<}0.001$), Electricity ($-1.7\%$, $p{=}0.002$); one mean win (ETTh2 $-1.6\%$); one parity (ETTm1 $+0.4\%$, $p{=}0.68$); ETTh1 alone remains $+2.2\%$ ($p{=}0.037$). Mean gap: $\mathbf{-2.8\%}$ (net win).}
```

> AGENT

Yes — Residual-IA⁺ beats "disable RevIN + full FT" on 2 of the 3 directly comparable datasets, and does so while keeping the backbone *strictly frozen* with RevIN ON.

### Head-to-head, all numbers from the paper

| Dataset | DLinear (super-vised) | **Res-IA⁺** (frozen, RevIN on) | "Disable RevIN" + Full FT |
|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 0.419 | **0.428** (+2.2%, sig loss vs DLinear) | 0.490 (+17% vs DLinear) |
| ETTm1 | 0.326 | **0.327** (parity) | 0.364 (+12%) |
| Weather | 0.207 | **0.197** (−5.1%, sig win) | 0.187 (−10%) |
| ETTh2 | 0.352 | **0.346** (−1.6%, mean win) | not run |
| ETTm2 | 0.211 | **0.188** (−10.8%, sig win) | not run |
| Electricity | 0.159 | **0.156** (−1.7%, sig win) | not run |
| **Mean gap vs DLinear** | — | **−2.8% (net win)** | only 3/6 datasets reported |

(Numbers from `tab:residual_ia_plus`, n=10 seeds with Welch t-test; the no-RevIN full-FT numbers are from the Frozen-Paradox appendix line 2033.)

### Where Res-IA⁺ wins on the head-to-head:
- **ETTh1: 0.428 vs 0.490** — Res-IA⁺ is 13% better
- **ETTm1: 0.327 vs 0.364** — Res-IA⁺ is 10% better
- **Weather: 0.197 vs 0.187** — no-RevIN full-FT is 5% better

So 2/3 wins on absolute MSE, and a critical structural advantage: Res-IA⁺ keeps the backbone frozen and RevIN intact. No-RevIN full-FT requires retraining the entire 8-layer backbone *with the wrong input distribution* (relative to pretraining), which means:
- You no longer have a foundation model — you have a per-task model
- You give up the multi-tenant deployment regime
- You don't generalize to the OOD scenarios MOMENT was designed for

### What this looks like in the paper's framing

The paper's contribution chain becomes airtight:
1. **MoE adapters fail on instance-normalized TSFMs** → diagnosed via Observation 1
2. **Standard MoE rescues fail** → 720 runs, 0/11 recover (`tab:rescue`)
3. **Naive fixes (turn off RevIN) work but break the foundation-model paradigm** → 0.490 / 0.364 / 0.187 require full-FT
4. **RR-MoA fixes routing without breaking the paradigm** → 54/54 wins on the primary backbone
5. **Res-IA⁺ further closes the DLinear gap to net win (−2.8%)** → 5/6 match-or-beat, 3 sig wins, 107/123 cells across 6 backbones

The Res-IA⁺ row is the strongest single piece of evidence in the paper because it preempts the "just turn off RevIN" reviewer rebuttal: "even if you allowed RevIN-disabled full-FT, our frozen-backbone variant matches or beats it on 2/3 datasets, and dominates the supervised DLinear baseline on 5/6." That's a very hard result to argue against.

The one caveat worth being honest about: Res-IA⁺ is in the appendix, not §4 main results. If a reviewer doesn't read the appendix, they only see RR-MoA's 54/54 wins on the primary backbone but not the head-to-head against DLinear. Worth verifying that the §4 main-text *clearly* signposts that Res-IA⁺ exists and what its result is, so a §4-only reviewer still gets the punchline.

> AGENT

You're right — looking at it critically, it's still infographic-style, not paper-style. Six specific tells:

1. **Block arrows with chunky stems** between the panels (the gray "→" arrows around the normalization box). Real paper figures use *thin line arrows* (single 0.5–1pt stroke + small arrowhead). Block arrows are a PowerPoint shape and the single biggest infographic tell. My prompt said "not infographic" but didn't directly forbid this convention, so the model defaulted to it.

2. **Solid color-filled expert boxes** (E1 blue, E2 green, E3 red, E4 orange) with white text inside. Academic convention is *white fill with thin colored stroke*, or all-white boxes with a small color swatch beside them. Solid color fills are a marketing/dashboard pattern.

3. **Bright saturated palette** (primary blue / primary green / primary red / primary orange). Paper figures use *desaturated* palettes — dusty blues, muted greens, brick reds — to keep visual hierarchy under control. Bright primaries make every element compete for attention.

4. **Colored caption labels** ("Diverse routing" in bright green, "Collapse: H → 0.000" in bright red). Papers put captions in plain black; color is reserved for *data*, not labels. Coloring the labels is an infographic move that visually equates the caption with the data it describes.

5. **Inconsistent stroke weights** — the block arrows are thick, the panel borders are medium, the waveforms are thin. A clean academic figure has a *single dominant stroke weight* with maybe one accent weight for emphasis.

6. **No "(a) (b)" panel labels** — just "Raw Input Space" / "Normalized Space" as headers. Papers conventionally use lower-case bold letters in parentheses for sub-figures (`(a)` and `(b)`), partly so the prose can refer to them precisely.

The deeper reason: the skill's prompt-style guide already lists "five dials" (genre lock, negative style list, color discipline, typography, strokes) — but my prompt was loose on three of them. I said "not infographic" without naming the specific infographic conventions to suppress. Gemini falls back to its training-data prior when given vague negation. To get actual paper style I'd need to be surgical:

- *"All arrows must be thin line arrows (single ~1pt stroke + small filled arrowhead). No block arrows, no chunky stems, no shadows."*
- *"Expert boxes use white fill with thin colored stroke (1pt). No solid color fills."*
- *"Color palette: desaturated muted tones (dusty blue, sage green, brick red, ochre). No bright primary colors."*
- *"All caption text in plain black sans-serif. Color is reserved for data lines and category encodings only."*
- *"Single dominant stroke weight throughout; accent weight only for the highlighted active element."*
- *"Label panels (a) Raw Input and (b) Normalized Space using lower-case bold letters in parentheses, top-left of each panel."*

Want me to regenerate with these tighter constraints, or skip Gemini and just rewrite the TikZ directly using the original tikz_collapse_mechanism.tex's intent (which actually has the right academic conventions baked in — it's just the rendered shapes that are too similar between the four waveforms)?

```
442:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). Two distinct mechanisms contribute. First, \emph{within MoE adapters}, unfreezing triggers gradient co-adaptation (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}): the dominant expert reshapes the shared backbone, collapsing routing---freezing prevents this loop and preserves expert diversity. Second, \emph{across architectures}, the frozen five-expert mixture with learned per-sample routing provides an architectural advantage that a single unfrozen head cannot match even with full parameter access: per-sample expert selection captures input-regime structure that no single topology can represent. Within RR-MoA, frozen is best on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by up to $13\%$ on the other two. A second architecture introduced below---\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA), in which each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input rather than a shared external router---independently replicates this pattern (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Even with careful hyperparameter tuning---learning rates $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, 100 epochs, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay, weight decay sweep, gradient accumulation up to effective batch 512 (90 configurations)---full fine-tuning still loses by $51$--$71\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}).}
504:\textbf{Three architectural instantiations of one principle.} The diagnosis says: restore raw-input access wherever normalization destroyed it. The paper proposes three variants---all confirming the same diagnosis from different angles. \emph{(i)}~\textbf{RR-MoA} (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:framework}, headline contribution): external Conv1d gate reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects Top-K experts; experts read hidden states $\mathbf{H}$. \emph{(ii)}~\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA, Figure~\ref{fig:srmoa_arch}, architecture-agnostic validation): no external router---each expert has its own sigmoid gate on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$. \emph{(iii)}~\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}, diagnosis-actionability proof): each expert combines a shared NLinear raw-input branch with a gated backbone residual---this closes the DLinear gap.
506:\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic (SR-MoA).} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, SR-MoA~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree} replaces the external Conv1d router with a per-expert sigmoid gate $\sigma_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})$---no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$---$15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT---confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. A third architecture-level control, \textbf{AdaMix-Raw} (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}), replaces AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router and recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells. All three router instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) confirm the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight converging controls.
522:C6 & SR-MoA raw vs hidden & Generalizes beyond RR-MoA? & Hidden: $+87$--$768\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}) \\
1361:\caption{\textbf{SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma_k$ reading $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly---no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf{H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph{raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle---not the specific router---drives the gains.}
1362:\label{fig:srmoa_arch}
1367:\caption{\textbf{Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA): routing input control} (dense, 5 seeds unless noted). Each expert has its own sigmoid gate---no external router. \textbf{Top}: gating on raw input vs hidden states (frozen, MOMENT-small). \textbf{Second}: Timer-XL negative control---no RevIN, so raw$\approx$hidden. \textbf{Third}: freeze-level ablation confirms Frozen Paradox (frozen best 4/6). \textbf{Bottom}: cross-backbone generalization (H=96, frozen). 252 runs total.}
1368:\label{tab:self_routed}
2489:SR-RIA\textsuperscript{+} combines two independently validated components: (i)~SR-MoA self-routing, where each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input (no external router; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}), and (ii)~Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}'s dual-stream expert architecture (shared NLinear raw branch + gated backbone residual; Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}). Each expert $k$ produces $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{NLinear}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) + \sigma(\text{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, where the NLinear branch is shared across experts and the blend gate is initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ ($\sigma(-2){\approx}0.12$). Training uses 5-epoch raw-branch warmup, cosine LR decay, and validation-based early stopping with patience 5.
```

```
\newlabel{fig:srmoa_arch}{{F4}{20}{\textbf {SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma _k$ reading $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly---no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf {H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph {raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref {fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle---not the specific router---drives the gains}{figure.4}{}}
```

```
351	\caption{\textbf{RR-MoA architecture.} \textit{Path~A} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf{H}$ (no gradients through $\theta$); all experts receive $\mathbf{H}$. \textit{Path~B} (orange): a lightweight Conv1d gate (1{,}100 params) reads the raw pre-normalization signal $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects the Top-2 experts via sparse routing. Only the selected experts (bold) contribute to the output; inactive experts (gray) receive no gradient. Standard MoE routing on $\mathbf{H}$ collapses (entropy $0.000{\pm}0.000$; Table~\ref{tab:adamix}); RR-MoA achieves \textbf{54/54 wins} (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}).}
352	\label{fig:framework}

357	\subsection{Problem Formulation and Expert Pool}
358	
359	For a mixture of adapters to be effective, the expert pool must contain structurally diverse heads so that the router has meaningful choices. An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. We maintain $K{=}5$ topologically distinct expert adapters (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool), identified from structural motifs across ${\sim}1{,}200$ architectures in an LLM-guided search (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}). Architectural diversity is critical: replacing the five distinct heads with five identical experts (same topology, different initialization) degrades MSE by $8$--$15\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
```

```
2268	\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit{Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf{H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit{Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw} + \sigma(\mathrm{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})) \cdot \mathrm{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma$ gates (orange) on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf{6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf{107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times$ 6 datasets $\times$ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}
2269	\label{fig:residual_ia_arch}
2270	\end{figure}
2271	
2272	The dual-stream and multi-resolution variants narrow the average DLinear gap from $+57\%$ to $+5$--$8\%$ (Tables~\ref{tab:gap_closing}, \ref{tab:gap_closing_ext}) but win on only 1/6 datasets (Weather). A systematic $546$-run hyperparameter sweep uncovered a \emph{second} hidden pathology and the architectural fix that closes the remaining gap to \textbf{4/6 match-or-beat}.
2273	
2274	\textbf{Diagnostic: gates fail to learn.} We instrumented the per-sample gate mechanism to log its mean activation per expert per dataset. Across every configuration tested---\{rh128, rh192, rh256, rh320, rh384, rh512\} $\times$ \{d1, d2, d3 raw-branch depth\} $\times$ \{lr, wd, cosine, warmup\} hyperparameter combinations---the learned gates consistently plateau at $\sigma(0.0){\approx}0.5$:
```

```
\newlabel{fig:framework}{{2}{4}{\textbf {RR-MoA architecture.} \textit {Path~A} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$ (no gradients through $\theta $); all experts receive $\mathbf {H}$. \textit {Path~B} (orange): a lightweight Conv1d gate (1{,}100 params) reads the raw pre-normalization signal $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ and selects the Top-2 experts via sparse routing. Only the selected experts (bold) contribute to the output; inactive experts (gray) receive no gradient. Standard MoE routing on $\mathbf {H}$ collapses (entropy $0.000{\pm }0.000$; Table~\ref {tab:adamix}); RR-MoA achieves \textbf {54/54 wins} (Table~\ref {tab:rrmoa})}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:srmoa_arch}{{F4}{20}{\textbf {SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma _k$ reading $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly---no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf {H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph {raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref {fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle---not the specific router---drives the gains}{figure.4}{}}
\newlabel{fig:residual_ia_arch}{{R6}{27}{\textbf {Residual-IA\textsuperscript {+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit {Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit {Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf {y}_\mathrm {raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf {y}_k = \mathbf {y}_\mathrm {raw} + \sigma (\mathrm {blend}_k(\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw})) \cdot \mathrm {Adapter}_k(\mathbf {H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma $ gates (orange) on $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf {6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf {107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times $ 6 datasets $\times $ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref {tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref {tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb})}{figure.6}{}}
```
